# How to use this guide

Pharmaceutical Jurisprudence is a **memory and structure** subject. There are no numericals except the DPCO ceiling-price calculation. Marks come from writing answers in a clear legal format: the **name and year of the Act**, its **objectives**, the **definition**, the **section number**, the **composition** of a body, and the **offence with its penalty**. Study one unit at a time: read the notes, write out the tables (schedules, licence forms, compositions, penalties) from memory, then answer the question bank. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short (5-mark) and long (10-mark) questions.

**Units in this guide** follow the five PCI units:

| Unit | Content | Syllabus hours |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules – objectives, definitions, schedules, import, manufacture | 10 |
| 2 | Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules – schedules in detail, sale, labelling, administration | 10 |
| 3 | Pharmacy Act, M&TP Act, NDPS Act | 10 |
| 4 | DMR Act, PCA Act and CPCSEA, NPPA, DPCO 2013, NLEM | 8 |
| 5 | Legislation history and committees, code of ethics, MTP Act, RTI Act, IPR | 7 |

Unit 3 holds three Acts and is longer than the others; it is kept as one unit to match the syllabus.

**Typical PCI end-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** Confirm the exact split with your college, since universities sometimes vary it.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long essays — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — asked in most years; prepare the full answer with tables and section numbers.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — rare, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from common patterns and syllabus weight, not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Definitions of misbranded, adulterated and spurious drugs; classes of drugs prohibited from import; conditions for grant of manufacturing licence; loan licence; section 27 penalties |
| 2 | Schedules G, H, H1, M, N, P, X, Y; types and conditions of sale licences; labelling; DTAB, DCC, CDL; powers and duties of drugs inspectors |
| 3 | PCI and State Council constitution and functions; Education Regulations; registration; NDPS definitions, Consultative Committee, National Fund, opium poppy cultivation, offences; M&TP in bond and outside bond |
| 4 | DMR prohibited advertisements and exemptions; CPCSEA/IAEC and guidelines; DPCO 2013 definitions, ceiling price calculation, NLEM |
| 5 | Drugs Enquiry, Bhore, Mudaliar and Hathi committees; code of ethics; MTP Act; RTI Act; IPR and patents |

**Laws change — what to check before the exam**

This subject is about **current law**, and several things in older textbooks are out of date:

1. **M&TP Act, 1955** was **repealed by section 174 of the CGST Act, 2017** (from 1 July 2017). Learn it, but say so in your answer.
2. **Pharmacy Act penalties** (sections 26A, 41, 42, 43) were changed by the **Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023**, in force from 31 December 2024, with a new **section 43A** for adjudication.
3. **Schedule Y** is replaced by the **New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019**; **Schedule M** was revised in December 2023; blood banks are now **blood centres**; medical devices have their own **Medical Devices Rules, 2017**.
4. **CPCSEA** was renamed **CCSEA** in 2023.
5. **NLEM 2022** (384 medicines) is the current First Schedule of DPCO 2013; a new list may come.
6. Drug bans under section 26A and licence form numbers change often.

Where a book and the official text differ, follow the official text on **cdsco.gov.in**, **indiacode.nic.in**, **pci.nic.in** and **nppaindia.nic.in**, and ask your teacher which version your university expects.

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Begin each answer with the **full name of the Act, its year**, and a one-line **objective**. Examiners give marks for this framing.
2. Quote **section numbers** where you are sure of them (section 3 PCI, 10 Education Regulations, 19 State Council, 32 registration; D&C 5 DTAB, 6 CDL, 7 DCC, 17/17A/17B, 18, 26A, 27; NDPS 6, 7A, 8, 27, 64A). A wrong number costs more than no number.
3. Put **compositions** of DTAB, DCC, PCI, State Council and the NDPS Consultative Committee in a **table**.
4. For offences, use a three-column table: **offence – section – penalty**.
5. For schedules, write **content + label + example** for each.
6. In DPCO questions, show the **ceiling price formula** with a small worked example.
7. End long answers with a line on **recent amendments** — it shows you know the current law.
8. Very short answers (2 marks): definition + one example or one number.

# Last-night revision sheet

If you have only an hour, learn these five answers well: **definitions of misbranded, adulterated and spurious drugs with section 27 penalties**, **schedules G, H, H1, M, N, X, Y**, **constitution and functions of the PCI**, **NDPS definitions, Consultative Committee and National Fund**, and **DPCO 2013 ceiling price with NLEM**. Together they cover most 10-mark questions.

## Acts and years

| Act / instrument | Year | One-line purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drugs and Cosmetics Act / Rules | 1940 / 1945 | Import, manufacture, sale of drugs and cosmetics |
| Pharmacy Act | 1948 | Profession, PCI, State Councils, registration |
| DMR (Objectionable Advertisements) Act | 1954 | Bans adverts for Schedule diseases and magic remedies |
| M&TP (Excise Duties) Act | 1955 | Excise on alcohol/narcotic preparations — **repealed 1 July 2017 (CGST Act s.174)** |
| Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act | 1960 | Animal welfare; Chapter IV experiments; CPCSEA → **CCSEA (2023)** |
| MTP Act | 1971 (amended 2021) | Safe, legal termination of pregnancy |
| NDPS Act | 1985 (amended 1989, 2001, 2014, 2021) | Narcotic and psychotropic control |
| RTI Act | 2005 | Citizens' right to information |
| DPCO | 2013 | Ceiling prices of NLEM medicines (under Essential Commodities Act, 1955) |
| NDCT Rules | 2019 | New drugs and clinical trials (replaced Schedule Y) |

## Drugs and Cosmetics Act — must-know

| Item | Key point |
| --- | --- |
| Misbranded (s.17) | Wrong or misleading label; disguised damage |
| Adulterated (s.17A) | Filthy, insanitary, poisonous container, non-permitted colour, harmful substance, reduced strength |
| Spurious (s.17B) | Imitation, false maker, fictitious company, substitution |
| s.10 / 10A | Prohibited imports / Government power to ban import |
| s.18 / 26A / 26B | Prohibited manufacture and sale / ban of drugs / emergency regulation |
| Licences | Mfg 25, 28, 25A/28A loan, 25B repack, 29 test; Sale 20/21 retail, 20B/21B wholesale, 20F/20G Sch X, 20A/21A restricted |
| Retail premises | 10 m² (15 m² with wholesale), refrigerator, registered pharmacist |

**Section 27 (2008 amendment)**

| Clause | Offence | Punishment |
| --- | --- | --- |
| (a) | Adulterated/spurious drug likely to cause death or grievous hurt | 10 years to life; fine ≥ ₹10 lakh or 3× value |
| (b) | Adulterated drug; no licence | 3–5 years; fine ≥ ₹1 lakh or 3× value |
| (c) | Spurious drug | 7 years to life; fine ≥ ₹3 lakh or 3× value |
| (d) | Other contraventions | 1–2 years; fine ≥ ₹20,000 (compoundable since Jan Vishwas 2023) |

**Schedules**

| Schedule | Content | Label / rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| G | Use under medical supervision | "Caution: It is dangerous to take this preparation except under medical supervision" |
| H | Prescription drugs | Rx + "To be sold by retail on the prescription of a RMP only"; NRx if also NDPS |
| H1 | 3rd/4th-gen antibiotics, anti-TB, some habit-forming | Rx in red, boxed warning; register kept 3 years |
| X | High-misuse psychotropic/narcotic | XRx; duplicate prescription kept 2 years; lock and key |
| M | GMP (revised Dec 2023) | Condition of manufacturing licence |
| N | Pharmacy equipment, books, premises | IP, NFI, D&C Act and Rules |
| P / P1 | Shelf life / pack sizes | |
| T | GMP for ASU | |
| U | Manufacturing and analytical records | |
| V | Vitamin/mineral standards for patent medicines | |
| Y | Clinical trials → NDCT Rules 2019 | |
| Part XII B / F | Blood banks → blood centres | Testing for HIV, HBV, HCV, syphilis, malaria |
| J | Diseases no drug may claim to cure | |

**Administration:** DTAB (s.5, chairman DGHS, technical advice) · CDL (s.6, Kolkata, final appellate test) · DCC (s.7, 2 Central + 1 per State, uniformity) · Government Analyst (s.20) · Inspector (s.21–23: inspect, sample in 4 parts, search, seize) · Licensing: DCGI (central), State Drugs Controller.

## Pharmacy Act — must-know

| PCI (s.3) | State Council (s.19) |
| --- | --- |
| 6 elected by UGC (teachers: pharm chem, pharmacy, pharmacology, pharmacognosy) | 6 elected by registered pharmacists |
| 6 nominated by Centre (≥4 pharmacy qualified) | 5 nominated by State (≥3 pharmacy qualified) |
| 1 elected by MCI (now NMC) | 1 elected by State Medical Council |
| DGHS, Drugs Controller of India, Director CDL (ex officio) | Chief administrative medical officer, drugs control officer, Government Analyst (ex officio) |
| 1 rep each of UGC and AICTE | |
| 1 elected per State Council + 1 nominated per State | |

s.10 Education Regulations · s.12 approval · s.13 withdrawal · s.32 registration (18 years, approved qualification, fee) · s.36 removal · Offences: 26A obstructing inspector, 41 false claim, 42 unregistered dispensing, 43 not surrendering certificate — **penalties revised by Jan Vishwas Act 2023 (from 31 Dec 2024), new s.43A adjudication**.

## NDPS Act — must-know

- s.4 Central Govt (NCB 1986) · s.5 Narcotics Commissioner · **s.6 Consultative Committee: Chairman + up to 20 members, advisory** · **s.7A National Fund for Control of Drug Abuse (1989)** · s.8 prohibition except medical/scientific use · s.9 Central powers · s.10 State powers.
- Narcotic drug = coca leaf, cannabis, opium, poppy straw, manufactured drugs; psychotropic = substances in the Schedule.
- Opium: licensed cultivators (MP, Rajasthan, UP) tender opium to CBN → Government Opium and Alkaloid Works (Ghazipur, Neemuch) → export only by Government.

| Quantity | Punishment |
| --- | --- |
| Small | RI up to 1 year or fine up to ₹10,000 or both |
| Intermediate | RI up to 10 years + fine up to ₹1 lakh |
| Commercial | RI 10–20 years + fine ₹1–2 lakh |

s.27 consumption (1 year/₹20,000 for cocaine, morphine, heroin; 6 months/₹10,000 others) · s.27A financing 10–20 years · s.31 repeat 1.5× · s.31A death (discretionary since 2014) · s.64A immunity for addicts seeking treatment.

## Other Acts

- **DMR Act:** s.3 adverts for miscarriage, contraception, sexual pleasure, menstrual disorder, **54 Schedule diseases**; s.4 misleading; s.5 magic remedy (talisman, mantra, kavacha, charm); s.14 exemptions (RMP signboard, scientific book, confidential to doctors, Government); s.7 penalty 6 months (first) / 1 year (subsequent).
- **PCA Act:** s.14–20 experiments; s.15 CPCSEA (now CCSEA); IAEC; 3 Rs (Replacement, Reduction, Refinement) + Rehabilitation; registration; records; s.19 suspend/revoke; s.20 penalty.
- **DPCO 2013:** ceiling price = simple average PTR of brands with ≥1% market share + **16%** retailer margin; revised every **1 April** by **WPI**; non-scheduled MRP rise ≤ **10%/year**; para 19 extraordinary circumstances; NPPA (1997) enforces; **NLEM 2022 = 384 medicines, 27 categories**.
- **MTP Act (2021):** ≤20 weeks 1 RMP; 20–24 weeks 2 RMPs (special categories); >24 weeks foetal abnormality via Medical Board; written consent (guardian for minor); s.5A confidentiality.
- **RTI Act:** ₹10; 30 days; 48 hours for life/liberty; first appeal 30 days; second appeal 90 days to CIC/SIC; penalty ₹250/day up to ₹25,000; s.8 exemptions.
- **IPR:** patent 20 years (novelty, inventive step, industrial application); s.3(d) (Novartis 2013); s.84 compulsory licence (Natco–Bayer 2012); s.107A Bolar; trademark 10 years renewable; copyright life + 60; design 10 + 5; GI 10 renewable.
- **Committees:** Drugs Enquiry (Chopra, 1930–31) → D&C Act; Bhore (1943–46); Mudaliar (1959–61); Hathi (1974–75: 117 essential drugs, generic names, National Drug Authority).
- **Code of ethics:** pharmacist in relation to job, trade, medical profession, profession; pharmacist's oath.

questions.answer:
1. Introduction: D&C Act 1940 regulates import, manufacture, distribution and sale; sections 17, 17A, 17B define the three categories.
2. Misbranded (s.17): coloured, coated, powdered or polished to conceal damage or look better; not labelled as prescribed; label or container carries a false or misleading claim.
3. Adulterated (s.17A): filthy, putrid or decomposed substance; made, packed or stored in insanitary conditions; container of poisonous substance; non-permitted colour; harmful or toxic substance; substance mixed to reduce quality or strength.
4. Spurious (s.17B): sold under the name of another drug (imitation/substitute); pretends to be the product of another maker; fictitious manufacturer; substituted wholly or partly; claims to be product of a maker who did not make it.
5. Section 18 prohibits manufacture, sale, stocking and distribution of such drugs.
6. Penalties (s.27 after 2008): (a) adulterated/spurious drug likely to cause death or grievous hurt — 10 years to life, fine not less than ₹10 lakh or 3× value of drugs confiscated, paid as compensation to victim/relatives; (b) adulterated drug or no licence — 3–5 years, fine ≥ ₹1 lakh or 3× value; (c) spurious drug — 7 years to life, fine ≥ ₹3 lakh or 3× value; (d) other contraventions — 1–2 years, fine ≥ ₹20,000.
7. Other features: offences under 27(a) and (c) cognizable and non-bailable; special courts; prosecution by inspector, gazetted officer, aggrieved person or consumer association; repeat offences (s.30) heavier; compounding (s.32B), widened by the Jan Vishwas Act 2023.
8. Conclusion: confiscation of stock and cancellation of licence also follow.
questions.question: Define misbranded, adulterated and spurious drugs under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. Discuss the penalties for manufacture and sale of such drugs as amended in 2008.

questions.answer:
1. Authority: Central Licensing Authority (DCGI, CDSCO); port offices check consignments.
2. Classes prohibited (s.10): not of standard quality; misbranded, adulterated, spurious; patent/proprietary medicine without true formula on label; drug claiming to cure Schedule J diseases; harmful cosmetic; drugs prohibited in country of origin or by rules; import without licence.
3. Section 10A: Government may prohibit import of drugs involving risk or lacking claimed therapeutic value; import of cosmetics tested on animals also prohibited.
4. Import under licence: registration certificate of foreign manufacturer and product; import licence for drugs other than Schedule X; separate licence for Schedule X; test licence for examination, test or analysis; small quantities for a patient's personal use with prescription; new drugs and clinical trial material under NDCT Rules 2019; devices under Medical Devices Rules 2017.
5. Conditions: proper premises and storage, manufacturer's test report with each consignment, minimum residual shelf life, allow inspection, keep records, report changes.
6. Offences (s.13): import of spurious/adulterated drugs — imprisonment and fine (heavier); other contraventions — lighter penalty, compoundable under s.32B; repeat offences higher; goods confiscated (s.14).
7. Note: form numbers and amounts are revised often; check the current rules.
questions.question: Describe the provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules regarding import of drugs: classes of drugs prohibited from import, import under licence or permit, and offences.

questions.answer:
1. Licensing authority: State Licensing Authority; Central Licence Approving Authority (DCGI) for Schedule C/C(1), LVPs, vaccines, sera, blood products.
2. Licence types: 25 (drugs other than C, C1, X), 28 (C and C1), 25A/28A loan, 25B repacking, 29 test.
3. Conditions for grant: premises, plant and equipment as per Schedule M; manufacture under active direction of qualified technical staff (degree in pharmacy/pharmaceutical chemistry/chemistry with experience); independent QC department with qualified analyst and laboratory; storage facilities; inspection before grant.
4. Conditions of licence: keep Schedule U records; test every batch; keep reference samples; allow inspection and sampling; report changes; recall substandard batches; comply with Schedule M; pay retention fee (licences no longer lapse after a fixed term).
5. Loan licence: given to a person without own factory who uses premises, equipment and staff of a licensed manufacturer; host must have spare capacity and agree; both responsible for quality.
6. Repacking licence: breaking bulk into small packs for retail; suitable premises; competent person; correct labels with original maker's details and batch; records; some categories excluded.
questions.question: Explain the conditions for grant of a licence to manufacture drugs and the conditions of the licence. Add notes on loan licence and repacking licence.

questions.answer:
1. Regulate import, manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs and cosmetics through licences.
2. Ensure drugs and cosmetics are safe, effective and of standard quality.
3. Prevent sale of substandard, misbranded, adulterated and spurious products.
4. Regulate Ayurvedic, Siddha, Unani and homoeopathic drugs.
5. Set up DTAB, DCC, CDL and similar ASU bodies.
6. Provide for inspectors, government analysts, offences and penalties.
7. Based on the recommendations of the Drugs Enquiry Committee (1930–31).
questions.question: Write the objectives of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940.

questions.answer:
Act: First Schedule — authoritative ASU books; Second Schedule — standards for drugs.
Rules: A — forms; B — fees for testing; C/C(1) — biological and special products; D — import exemptions; E(1) — poisonous ASU substances; F — biologicals and (Part XII B) blood centres; G — use under medical supervision; H/H1 — prescription drugs; J — diseases no drug may claim to cure; K — exemptions; M — GMP; N — pharmacy equipment; O — disinfectant fluids; P/P1 — shelf life/pack sizes; Q — coal tar colours for cosmetics; R — mechanical contraceptives; S — cosmetic standards; T — ASU GMP; U — manufacturing and analytical records; V — standards for patent medicines; X — high-misuse drugs; Y — clinical trials (now NDCT Rules 2019).
questions.question: Give the legal definitions of the schedules to the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules (any ten).

questions.answer:
1. Licence (traditionally Form 29) to make small quantities of a drug for research, development, stability studies or trial supply.
2. Conditions: drug not to be sold; quantities limited to need; for a stated period; under a qualified person; records of production, use and disposal kept and shown to inspectors; premises and equipment suitable; licensing authority informed of results where required; unused material destroyed properly.
3. Different from manufacture of a new drug, which needs permission of the Central Licensing Authority under NDCT Rules 2019 before commercial manufacture.
questions.question: What is meant by manufacture of a drug for examination, test or analysis? Write the conditions of such a licence.

questions.answer:
1. Section 18 prohibits manufacture for sale, sale, stocking, exhibiting or distribution of: drugs or cosmetics not of standard quality, misbranded, adulterated or spurious; patent/proprietary medicines without true formula; drugs claiming to cure Schedule J diseases; products made in breach of the Act; products without licence.
2. Section 26A: Central Government, after consulting DTAB, may regulate, restrict or prohibit a drug or cosmetic that involves risk to humans or animals, lacks claimed therapeutic value or has no therapeutic justification for its ingredients (used to ban irrational FDCs).
3. Section 26B (2008): regulate or restrict a drug in emergencies like epidemics or natural calamities.

# Unit 1: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules, 1945 – I

The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 (the D&C Act) is the main law that controls the **import, manufacture, distribution and sale** of drugs and cosmetics in India. The Act lays down the broad rules; the **Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945** give the details (licence forms, fees, schedules, labels). This unit covers the objectives, definitions, schedules, import and manufacture. Unit 2 covers the remaining schedules, sale, labelling and the administration of the Act.

> **Law changes.** The Rules are amended many times a year by notifications (G.S.R.) of the Ministry of Health. Form numbers, fees, schedules and some penalties quoted in older textbooks have changed. Before an exam, compare your textbook with the current Act and Rules on the CDSCO website (cdsco.gov.in) or India Code (indiacode.nic.in).

## 1.1 Background and objectives

The Act came from the recommendations of the **Drugs Enquiry Committee (1930–31)**, chaired by Col. R. N. Chopra (Unit 5). It was first called the Drugs Act, 1940; amendments in the 1960s brought in cosmetics (the Act was renamed the Drugs and Cosmetics Act) and Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani drugs.

**Objectives**

1. To regulate the **import, manufacture, distribution and sale** of drugs and cosmetics through **licences** and **permits**.
2. To make sure that drugs and cosmetics sold in India are **safe, effective and of standard quality**.
3. To prevent sale of **substandard, misbranded, adulterated and spurious** drugs and cosmetics.
4. To regulate Ayurvedic, Siddha, Unani (ASU) and Homoeopathic drugs as well as allopathic drugs.
5. To set up advisory and testing bodies: the **Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB)**, the **Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC)**, the **Central Drugs Laboratory (CDL)** and similar bodies for ASU drugs.
6. To provide for **inspectors and government analysts** and to lay down **offences and penalties**.

## 1.2 Important definitions

| Term | Meaning in simple words |
| --- | --- |
| **Drug** | All medicines for internal or external use of human beings or animals, and substances used in the diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease; substances (other than food) meant to affect the structure or function of the body; substances used against vermin or insects that cause disease; components of drugs such as empty capsules; and **devices notified** by the Central Government |
| **Cosmetic** | Any article meant to be rubbed, poured, sprinkled, sprayed or applied to the body for **cleansing, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering appearance**; includes components of cosmetics |
| **Ayurvedic, Siddha or Unani drug** | Medicines made exclusively according to the formulae in the authoritative books listed in the **First Schedule** of the Act |
| **Patent or proprietary medicine** | (Allopathic) a drug that is a remedy or prescription presented in a form ready for internal or external use and **not included in the current Indian Pharmacopoeia** or other recognised pharmacopoeia; (ASU) a drug in a ready form with ingredients from the authoritative books but not itself a classical formula |
| **Manufacture** | Any process or part of a process for making, altering, ornamenting, finishing, packing, labelling, breaking up or otherwise treating a drug or cosmetic with a view to sale or distribution. It does **not** include compounding or dispensing in the ordinary course of retail business |
| **Government Analyst** | A person appointed under section 20 to test samples |
| **Inspector** | A person appointed under section 21 to enforce the Act |
| **Import** | Bringing into India |

### Misbranded, adulterated and spurious drugs

| Category (section) | A drug is in this category if… |
| --- | --- |
| **Misbranded** (17) | It is coloured, coated, powdered or polished so that damage is concealed or it looks better than it is; it is **not labelled as prescribed**; or its label or container carries a **false or misleading** statement or claim |
| **Adulterated** (17A) | It consists of a **filthy, putrid or decomposed** substance; it was made or stored in **insanitary conditions**; its container is made of a **poisonous** substance; it has a colour other than a **permitted colour**; it contains a **harmful or toxic** substance; or a substance has been **mixed to reduce its quality or strength** |
| **Spurious** (17B) | It is sold under the **name of another drug** (imitation or substitute); it **pretends to be the product of a manufacturer** who did not make it; it bears the name of a **fictitious** manufacturer or company; it has been **substituted** wholly or partly by another drug; or it claims to be the product of a manufacturer of whom it is not truly a product |

Cosmetics have parallel definitions (misbranded, spurious and adulterated cosmetics — sections 17C, 17D and 17E).

```text
Not of standard quality  -> fails the standards in the Second Schedule (IP, etc.)
Misbranded               -> wrong or misleading label / presentation
Adulterated              -> bad material or bad conditions of making / storing
Spurious                 -> fake identity (imitation, false maker, substitution)
```

## 1.3 Schedules to the Act and to the Rules

The **Act** has two schedules:

| Schedule of the Act | Content |
| --- | --- |
| **First Schedule** | List of authoritative books of Ayurveda, Siddha and Unani systems |
| **Second Schedule** | **Standards** to be followed by imported and manufactured drugs (for example, Indian Pharmacopoeia standards for official drugs; label claim and formula for patent or proprietary medicines) |

The **Rules** have many schedules. Their **legal definitions** (what each schedule covers) are a common short question:

| Schedule (Rules) | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| A | Forms of applications, licences, certificates and reports |
| B | Fees for testing or analysis by the CDL and State laboratories |
| C and C(1) | Biological and special products (vaccines, sera, insulin, parenterals; digitalis and ergot preparations, ophthalmic preparations, etc.) needing special licences |
| D | Exemptions in respect of import of certain drugs |
| E(1) | Poisonous substances under ASU systems (warning labels) |
| F | Requirements for vaccines, sera and other biologicals; its Part XII B covers **blood banks (now called blood centres)** and Part XII C covers blood products from human plasma |
| F(1), F(2), F(3), F(F) | Standards for vaccines, sera, surgical dressings, umbilical tapes, ophthalmic preparations |
| G | Drugs to be used **under medical supervision** (caution label) |
| H and H1 | **Prescription drugs**; H1 = specified antibiotics, anti-TB and habit-forming drugs with a register |
| J | Diseases and ailments that **no drug may claim to prevent or cure** |
| K | Drugs and situations **exempted** from certain provisions |
| M, M-I to M-III | **Good Manufacturing Practices** (allopathic, homoeopathic, devices) |
| N | Minimum equipment for efficient running of a **pharmacy** |
| O | Standards for disinfectant fluids |
| P, P1 | **Life period** (shelf life) of drugs and pack sizes |
| Q | Permitted coal tar colours in cosmetics; cosmetic standards |
| R | Standards for mechanical contraceptives |
| S | Standards for cosmetics |
| T | GMP for **Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani** medicines |
| U, U(1) | Particulars of **manufacturing and analytical records** (drugs; cosmetics) |
| V | Standards for **patent or proprietary medicines** (vitamin and mineral content) |
| W | (Now omitted) generic names of drugs to be marketed under generic names |
| X | **Narcotic and psychotropic drugs** with high misuse potential, needing special licences |
| Y | Requirements for clinical trials and import or manufacture of **new drugs** — now replaced by the **New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019** |

Schedules G, H, M, N, P, T, U, V, X, Y and Part XII B with Schedule F are studied in detail in Unit 2.

## 1.4 Import of drugs and cosmetics

### Classes of drugs and cosmetics prohibited from import (section 10)

No one may import:

1. A drug or cosmetic that is **not of standard quality**.
2. A **misbranded**, **adulterated** or **spurious** drug, or a misbranded or spurious cosmetic.
3. A **patent or proprietary medicine** whose label does not show the true formula or list of active ingredients with quantities.
4. A drug that claims to **cure or mitigate a disease named in Schedule J** (or claims it falsely).
5. A **cosmetic** containing an ingredient that may make it unsafe or harmful under the directions for use.
6. Any drug or cosmetic whose import is **prohibited by the rules** (for example, drugs whose manufacture, sale or distribution is **prohibited in the country of origin**, except for certain approved purposes).
7. Any drug or cosmetic imported **without a licence** where one is needed.

Under **section 10A**, the Central Government can **prohibit import** of any drug or cosmetic that is likely to involve risk to people or animals, or that does not have the therapeutic value claimed. The Rules also prohibit import of **cosmetics tested on animals** (a 2014 amendment).

### Import under licence or permit

```text
Foreign manufacturer --(registration of site + product)--> Registration Certificate
            |
Indian importer --(applies to the Licensing Authority = DCGI, CDSCO)--> Import licence
            |
Customs ports with CDSCO port offices check every consignment
```

| Purpose of import | What is needed (older form numbers in brackets — check current rules) |
| --- | --- |
| Import of drugs for **sale** (other than Schedule X) | Registration certificate of the foreign maker and product, and an **import licence** (Form 10) |
| Import of **Schedule X** drugs | Separate licence (Form 10A) |
| Import for **examination, test or analysis** | Test licence (Form 11), small quantities, not for sale |
| Import for **personal use** of a patient | Small quantities for a patient's own use, with a prescription, are allowed under the conditions in the rules; larger quantities need a permit |
| Import of **new drugs** or for **clinical trials** | Permission under the **New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019** |
| Import of **medical devices** | Licence under the **Medical Devices Rules, 2017** |

**Conditions of an import licence** (main points): the importer must have premises with proper storage; must allow inspection; each consignment must carry the manufacturer's test report; drugs must have the prescribed **residual shelf life** at import; the importer must report any change and keep records of sales.

### Offences and penalties on import (section 13)

- Import of a **spurious or adulterated** drug (and of a drug or cosmetic that is not of standard quality in some cases) is punishable with **imprisonment and fine**, and the goods are **confiscated** (section 14).
- Import of any other drug or cosmetic in contravention of the Act attracts a smaller penalty, which can be **compounded** under section 32B (inserted in 2008).
- **Repeat offences** carry higher punishment.

The amounts for section 13 have been revised over the years; learn the pattern (spurious/adulterated = heavier; other breaches = lighter, compoundable) and check the current figures in the bare Act.

## 1.5 Manufacture of drugs

### Prohibition of manufacture and sale of certain drugs (section 18)

No person shall manufacture for sale, sell, stock, exhibit for sale or distribute:

1. A drug that is **not of standard quality**, or is **misbranded, adulterated or spurious**.
2. A cosmetic that is not of standard quality, or is misbranded, adulterated or spurious.
3. A **patent or proprietary medicine** that does not display the true formula on the label.
4. A drug that claims to cure or prevent a **Schedule J** disease.
5. A drug or cosmetic in contravention of the Act or Rules.
6. Any drug or cosmetic **without a licence**.

**Section 26A** allows the Central Government (after consulting the DTAB) to **regulate, restrict or prohibit** manufacture and sale of a drug that involves risk, lacks the claimed therapeutic value or has no therapeutic justification (irrational fixed-dose combinations have been banned this way). **Section 26B** (inserted in 2008) lets the Government regulate or restrict a drug needed in an **emergency** such as an epidemic or natural calamity.

### Types of manufacturing licence

| Licence (traditional form number) | For |
| --- | --- |
| Form 25 | Drugs other than Schedules C, C(1) and X |
| Form 28 | Drugs in Schedules C and C(1) (not X) |
| Form 25A / 28A | **Loan licence** (same groups as above) |
| Form 25B | **Repacking** licence |
| Form 29 | Manufacture for **examination, test or analysis** |
| Form 28D | Large volume parenterals, sera, vaccines, blood products and similar items (with central approval) |
| Separate licences | Schedule X drugs, cosmetics, homoeopathic medicines, ASU drugs |

The **State Licensing Authority** grants most licences. For Schedule C/C(1) products, large volume parenterals, vaccines, sera and blood products, the licence also needs the approval of the **Central Licence Approving Authority (the Drugs Controller General of India)**. Under amendments made in 2017–18, most licences no longer expire after five years; they stay valid while the **retention fee** is paid at the set interval. Confirm the current rule.

### Conditions for the grant of a manufacturing licence

1. **Premises, plant and equipment** that meet **Schedule M** (GMP).
2. **Technical staff:** manufacture must be under the **active direction and personal supervision** of a competent person with a degree in pharmacy, pharmaceutical chemistry or chemistry (or medicine, for certain products) with the experience the rules lay down.
3. **Testing staff and laboratory:** a separate quality control section headed by a qualified person, with its own testing facilities.
4. **Adequate storage** for raw materials, intermediates and finished products.
5. **Inspection** of the premises by drugs inspectors (jointly with central inspectors for C/C(1) items) before the licence is granted.

### Conditions of the licence (to be followed after grant)

1. Maintain records of manufacture and analysis as given in **Schedule U**, for the period laid down.
2. **Test each batch** of raw materials and finished products; release only after QC approval.
3. Keep **reference (retained) samples** of each batch.
4. Allow inspectors to **enter, inspect and take samples**, and supply samples on demand.
5. Report changes in technical staff, premises or products.
6. Recall batches found not of standard quality and inform the licensing authority.
7. Comply with **Schedule M** at all times; label as per the rules.
8. Pay the licence **retention fee** on time.

### Manufacture of drugs for test, examination and analysis

A licence (Form 29) lets an institution or manufacturer make **small quantities** of a drug for research, stability studies, development or clinical trial supply. Conditions: the drug **cannot be sold**; quantities are limited; records of production, use and disposal must be kept; the licence is for a stated period; inspectors may check the records.

### Manufacture of a new drug

A **new drug** is one not yet approved in India for the proposed claims, or an approved drug with a **new indication, new dosage form, new route, new strength** or **new fixed-dose combination**, or certain biologicals. A new drug can be made for sale only after **permission of the Central Licensing Authority (DCGI)** under the **New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019**, usually based on clinical trial data. Only then does the State licensing authority add the product to the manufacturing licence. (Before 2019, this was governed by Rule 122 and **Schedule Y**.)

### Loan licence

```text
Loan licensee (owns the brand, no factory)
        |
        |  uses premises, equipment and technical staff of
        v
Licensed manufacturer (has a Form 25/28 licence)
        |
        v
Product made under the loan licence (Form 25A / 28A); both share responsibility for quality
```

The loan licensee must show that the host factory has spare capacity and agrees to make the products. The loan licensee's own technical staff may be required to supervise. Both firms are answerable for quality.

### Repacking licence

**Repacking** is breaking up a drug from a bulk container into **small packs** for retail sale (for example, tablets, powders or ointments repacked from bulk). It needs a separate repacking licence (Form 25B). Conditions: suitable premises, supervision by a competent person (pharmacist or equivalent), proper labelling with the original manufacturer's details and batch number, and records. Certain categories (such as Schedule C/C(1) products) may not be repacked under it.

## 1.6 Offences and penalties for manufacture and sale (section 27, as amended in 2008)

| Offence | Punishment |
| --- | --- |
| **27(a)** Manufacture, sale or distribution of an **adulterated or spurious drug** which, when used, is likely to cause **death or grievous hurt** | Imprisonment **not less than 10 years**, which may extend to **life**; fine **not less than ₹10 lakh or three times the value of the drugs confiscated**, whichever is more. The fine is paid as **compensation** to the victim or, if the person died, to the relatives |
| **27(b)** **Adulterated** drug (not covered by (a)), or drug made or sold **without a valid licence** | Imprisonment **3 to 5 years**; fine **not less than ₹1 lakh or three times the value**, whichever is more |
| **27(c)** **Spurious** drug (not covered by (a)) | Imprisonment **not less than 7 years**, may extend to **life**; fine **not less than ₹3 lakh or three times the value**, whichever is more |
| **27(d)** Any other contravention (for example, not of standard quality, breach of licence conditions) | Imprisonment **1 to 2 years** and fine **not less than ₹20,000** (the court may give less for special reasons) |

Other features added in 2008:

- Offences under 27(a) and 27(c) are **cognizable and non-bailable**.
- **Special courts** can be designated for these offences; trials are by a **Court of Session**.
- **Prosecution** can be started by an inspector, an authorised gazetted officer, the aggrieved person or a recognised consumer association.
- Some minor offences can be **compounded** (section 32B). The **Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023** extended compounding to more offences (including section 27(d)) and changed some other penalty provisions of this Act; check the current text.
- **Repeat offences** (section 30) carry higher minimum terms.

## Remember

- Act = framework; **Rules, 1945** = details. First Schedule = ASU books; Second Schedule = standards.
- **Misbranded** = label fault; **adulterated** = material or condition fault; **spurious** = false identity.
- Import: **section 10** prohibited classes, **10A** Government power to ban import; import licence via **CDSCO**; test licence for analysis; NDCT Rules 2019 for new drugs; Medical Devices Rules 2017 for devices.
- Manufacture: **section 18** prohibitions; **26A** ban; licences 25/28 (general/C,C1), 25A/28A (loan), 25B (repack), 29 (test).
- Conditions of licence: Schedule M premises, qualified staff, own QC, Schedule U records, inspection, retained samples.
- Section 27 after 2008: (a) death/grievous hurt **10 years–life, ≥₹10 lakh**; (b) **3–5 years, ≥₹1 lakh**; (c) spurious **7 years–life, ≥₹3 lakh**; (d) others **1–2 years, ≥₹20,000**.
- Rules and forms keep changing — always check the current CDSCO text.

# Unit 2: Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 and Rules, 1945 – II

This unit studies the schedules named in the syllabus in detail (G, H, M, N, P, T, U, V, X, Y, Part XII B with Schedule F, and the schedule of diseases under the Drugs and Magic Remedies Act read with Schedule J), then the licences for **sale**, **labelling and packing**, and the **administration** of the Act: DTAB, CDL, DCC, government analysts, licensing and controlling authorities, and drugs inspectors.

> **Law changes.** Schedule M was replaced by a revised Schedule M in December 2023 (G.S.R. 922(E)); Schedule Y was replaced for new drugs and clinical trials by the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019; blood banks are now called blood centres. Older books describe the earlier versions. Check the current rules on cdsco.gov.in.

## 2.1 Schedules in detail

### Schedule G — drugs to be used under medical supervision

- Drugs in this schedule may be sold **without a prescription**, but must carry the warning:

```text
Caution: It is dangerous to take this preparation except under medical supervision.
```

- Examples (as listed): certain **antihistamines** and **oral antidiabetic** drugs, and some other drugs where unsupervised use is risky.
- The retailer should record the sale details as the rules require.

### Schedule H — prescription drugs

- Sold by retail **only on the prescription of a Registered Medical Practitioner (RMP)**.
- Label: the symbol **Rx** at the top left corner and the warning:

```text
Schedule H drug – Warning: To be sold by retail on the prescription of a
Registered Medical Practitioner only.
```

- If the drug is also in the NDPS Act lists, the label carries **NRx** in red with the same warning.
- The pharmacist must dispense only the quantity prescribed, keep the sale details (patient, prescriber, drug, quantity, batch) and stamp the prescription so it is not reused.
- Examples: most **antibiotics**, **antihypertensives**, **corticosteroids**, **anticancer drugs**, hormones and many others.

### Schedule H1 (added in 2013, in force from 2014)

- Third and fourth generation **antibiotics** (for example, cefepime, meropenem, moxifloxacin), **anti-tuberculosis** drugs (isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) and some **habit-forming** drugs (for example, alprazolam, zolpidem, buprenorphine).
- Purpose: to slow **antimicrobial resistance** and curb misuse.
- Label: **Rx in red** and a warning in a box with a red border: it is dangerous to take the preparation except in accordance with medical advice, and it must not be sold without a prescription.
- The retailer keeps a **separate H1 register** (prescriber's name and address, patient's name, drug and quantity), kept for **three years**.

### Schedule X — narcotic and psychotropic drugs needing special care

- Drugs with high potential for misuse, for example **amphetamine**, **methylphenidate**, and barbiturates such as **amobarbital, pentobarbital and secobarbital** (the list is revised from time to time).
- Label: **XRx** in red with the Schedule H type warning.
- **Special licences** for manufacture, import, wholesale and retail.
- Retail sale only on a prescription **in duplicate**; the pharmacist keeps one copy for **two years**.
- Separate records of purchase and sale; drugs stored under **lock and key**.

### Schedule M — Good Manufacturing Practices (GMP)

Schedule M lays down GMP and the requirements of premises, plant and equipment for pharmaceutical products.

```text
Revised Schedule M (G.S.R. 922(E), Dec 2023)
Part I   General GMP: quality management system, quality risk management,
         product quality review, personnel, premises, equipment, sanitation,
         materials, documentation, production, QC, validation,
         complaints and recalls, self-inspection, contract work
Part I-A onward  Specific requirements for each dosage form
         (sterile products, oral solids, oral liquids, topicals, MDIs,
          active pharmaceutical ingredients, biologicals, etc.)
```

- The revised version brings Indian GMP close to **WHO GMP**, adding a **pharmaceutical quality system**, **quality risk management**, **product quality review**, **stability programmes**, **validation** and computerised systems.
- Large manufacturers had to comply first; small and medium firms (MSMEs) were given extended time (to 31 December 2025, on application). Check the current status.
- Schedule M-I covers homoeopathic medicines; M-II and M-III earlier covered cosmetics and devices (devices are now under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017).

### Schedule N — minimum equipment for a pharmacy

| Head | Requirement (main points) |
| --- | --- |
| Premises | Separated from living quarters; clean, well lit and ventilated; adequate area; dispensing section separate and closed to the public |
| Equipment | Balances and weights, measures, mortars and pestles, spatulas, funnels, beakers, water bath, refrigerator, ointment slab, suppository mould and similar items |
| Books | Current **Indian Pharmacopoeia**, **National Formulary of India**, and the Drugs and Cosmetics Act and Rules |
| Staff | A **registered pharmacist** in charge of compounding and dispensing |
| Materials | Drugs and containers as needed for the work done |

### Schedule P — life period of drugs

- Gives the **maximum life period** (shelf life from date of manufacture) and storage conditions for listed drugs, mostly antibiotics, vitamins and some biologicals.
- For drugs not listed, the shelf life is fixed by the manufacturer from **stability data** acceptable to the licensing authority.
- **Schedule P1** lists **pack sizes** for certain drugs.

### Schedule T — GMP for Ayurvedic, Siddha and Unani medicines

- Requirements of premises (location, raw material store, manufacturing areas, packing area, quality control area), **equipment** for each dosage form (for example, for churna, gutika, bhasma, asava–arishta, taila, ghrita), **raw material identification**, **personnel** with qualifications in the system, and **documentation**.
- Compliance is a condition of an ASU manufacturing licence.

### Schedule U — manufacturing and analytical records

- **Manufacturing records:** batch number, quantities of raw materials, dates, in-process checks, yield, names of persons who supervised, packing details.
- **Analytical records:** tests on raw materials and finished products, reference to standards, results and signature of the analyst.
- Kept for the period laid down in the rules and shown to inspectors on demand. **Schedule U(1)** covers records for cosmetics.

### Schedule V — standards for patent or proprietary medicines

- Gives limits (minimum and maximum) for **vitamins and minerals** in patent or proprietary preparations sold for prophylaxis or treatment, so that products are neither too weak nor dangerously strong.

### Schedule Y and the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019

Schedule Y laid down how **clinical trials** were to be run and how permission was granted for **import or manufacture of new drugs**: phases of trials, ethics committee approval, informed consent, reporting of serious adverse events and compensation.

Since **2019** these matters are governed by the **New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019**, which replaced Part XA and Schedule Y for new drugs and clinical trials. Key features: **registered ethics committees**, approval timelines, **informed consent** (with audio-video recording in specified cases), **compensation** for trial-related injury or death, and conditions for academic trials and for waiving local trials.

```text
Clinical trial phases
Phase I   -> small number of healthy volunteers; safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics
Phase II  -> patients; dose finding and early efficacy
Phase III -> large patient groups; confirm efficacy and safety (basis of approval)
Phase IV  -> after marketing; post-marketing surveillance
```

### Part XII B and Schedule F — blood banks (blood centres)

- **Part XII B** of the Rules sets out the licensing and working of **blood banks**, now called **blood centres**, and blood component and plasma processing units; **Schedule F (Part XII B)** gives the detailed requirements.
- Covers: licence (granted by the State authority with central approval), **accommodation**, **personnel** (medical officer, technical supervisor, nurse, technicians), **equipment**, **donor selection criteria** (age, weight, haemoglobin, interval between donations), **testing of every unit** (blood group, HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis, malaria), **storage temperatures**, **labelling**, records and **discard** of unsuitable units.
- **Schedule F (Part XII C)** covers manufacture of blood products from bulk human plasma.

### Diseases that drugs may not claim to cure — Schedule J and the DMR (OA) Act

- **Schedule J** lists diseases and ailments that no drug may **purport to prevent or cure** (for example, cancer, diabetes, blindness, epilepsy, paralysis, sexual impotence, premature ageing). Such claims make import and sale illegal under the D&C Act.
- The **Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954** has its own **Schedule** of diseases for which **advertisements** are prohibited (Unit 4). Schedule J controls **claims on the drug and its label**, the DMR(OA) Act controls **advertisements**.

## 2.2 Sale of drugs

### Kinds of sale licence

| Licence | For |
| --- | --- |
| Form 20 | Retail sale of drugs other than Schedules C, C(1) and X |
| Form 21 | Retail sale of Schedule C and C(1) drugs (not X) |
| Form 20B | Wholesale of drugs other than C, C(1) and X |
| Form 21B | Wholesale of Schedule C and C(1) drugs |
| Form 20F / 20G | Retail / wholesale of Schedule X drugs |
| Form 20A / 21A | **Restricted licence** (no pharmacist) |

The **State Licensing Authority** grants sale licences. Like manufacturing licences, they now remain in force while the retention fee is paid.

### Conditions for a retail sale licence

1. **Premises:** at least **10 square metres** for retail sale (at least **15 square metres** if retail and wholesale are combined), clean and suitable, with proper storage.
2. **Refrigerator** where drugs need storage at low temperature.
3. Sale under the **personal supervision of a registered pharmacist**.
4. H, H1 and X drugs sold **only on prescription**; prescriptions stamped and records kept.
5. Licence and the pharmacist's name displayed.
6. Expired and damaged drugs kept apart and not sold.

### Conditions for a wholesale licence

1. Adequate premises (same minimum area) and storage.
2. Business under the charge of a **competent person**: a registered pharmacist, or a graduate with one year's experience in dealing with drugs, or a person who has passed the SSC (or equivalent) examination with four years' experience in drug dealing (as the rules list).
3. Sale only to licensed dealers, hospitals, institutions and registered medical practitioners, with proper invoices showing batch numbers and expiry dates.

### Restricted licence

- For dealers who do not employ a pharmacist, usually in **villages** where no pharmacy exists, and for itinerant vendors.
- Allows sale of only **certain drugs** — mainly household remedies — in **original sealed packs** from licensed manufacturers; no opening, mixing or dispensing.

### Offences and penalties for sale

Sale offences fall under **section 27** (the same scale as manufacture, Unit 1): spurious or adulterated drugs causing death or grievous hurt carry the heaviest penalty; sale without a licence carries 3–5 years; other breaches (for example, selling a Schedule H drug without prescription, not keeping records) fall under 27(d). The licence can also be **suspended or cancelled** by the licensing authority.

## 2.3 Labelling and packing of drugs

### General labelling requirements (main points of Rule 96)

The label on the innermost container and every covering must show:

1. **Name of the drug** — the proper (generic) name, shown more prominently than any trade name.
2. **Net content** (weight, volume, number of units).
3. **Content of active ingredients** per dose unit or per stated quantity.
4. **Name and address of the manufacturer** (and of the marketer if different).
5. **Distinctive batch number**.
6. **Manufacturing licence number**.
7. **Date of manufacture** and **date of expiry**.
8. **Maximum retail price** (under DPCO and packaging rules).
9. Special warnings: Schedule symbol (Rx, NRx, XRx), "For external use only", "Not for injection", "Shake well before use", storage conditions.
10. For injections: route of administration, and for multi-dose containers the preservative used.

**Special labels** apply to Schedules G, H, H1 and X (2.1), to ASU drugs ("Ayurvedic/Siddha/Unani medicine"), to drugs for **veterinary use** ("Not for human use; for veterinary use only"), to **physician samples** ("Physician's sample – not to be sold"), and to drugs supplied to the **Government** ("Government supply – not for sale").

### Specimen label (tablet)

```text
+--------------------------------------------------+
| Rx                    PARACETAMOL TABLETS IP 500 mg|
| Each uncoated tablet contains: Paracetamol IP 500 mg|
| 10 tablets                                        |
| Dosage: As directed by the physician              |
| Store in a cool, dry place, protected from light  |
| Mfg. Lic. No.: ......     B. No.: ......           |
| Mfg. date: MM/YYYY        Exp. date: MM/YYYY      |
| M.R.P. ₹ ....  (incl. of all taxes)               |
| Manufactured by: name and full address            |
+--------------------------------------------------+
(Rx and the Schedule H warning appear only if the drug is in Schedule H.)
```

### Labelling of cosmetics (main points)

Name of the cosmetic, name and address of the manufacturer, **list of ingredients** (in descending order of quantity for most products), net content, batch number, manufacturing licence number, date of manufacture and **date of expiry** (or "use before"), warnings and directions for safe use where needed.

### Permitted colours

Only the colours **permitted by the rules** may be used in drugs (a non-permitted colour makes a drug adulterated). The permitted list includes natural colours such as **caramel, beta-carotene, chlorophyll, curcumin, riboflavin, annatto, saffron, titanium dioxide and iron oxides**, and synthetic colours such as **tartrazine, sunset yellow FCF, erythrosine, ponceau 4R, carmoisine, brilliant blue FCF, indigo carmine and fast green FCF**, with their aluminium lakes. Confirm the current list in the rules.

### Packing

- Containers must be suitable and must not react with the contents.
- Pack sizes of some drugs are fixed (**Schedule P1**).

### Offences and penalties

Misbranding by wrong labels is an offence under sections 17 and 18, punishable under section 27 (usually 27(d)). Using a **Government Analyst's report** for advertising is an offence under **section 29**.

## 2.4 Administration of the Act and Rules

```text
                    Central Government (Ministry of Health)
                                  |
     +---------------+-------------+---------------+------------------+
     |               |             |               |                  |
    DTAB            DCC           CDL        CDSCO headed by      Central drugs
 (technical     (uniform        (Kolkata;     the DCGI (Central    inspectors
  advice)       enforcement)    appellate     Licensing / Licence
                                testing)      Approving Authority)
                                  |
                       State Governments
                                  |
     State Drugs Controller (Licensing and Controlling Authority)
     State Government Analysts / State Drug Testing Laboratories
     State Drugs Inspectors
```

### Drugs Technical Advisory Board (DTAB) — section 5

- **Function:** advises the Central and State Governments on **technical matters** arising out of the administration of the Act (for example, banning drugs under section 26A, changes in schedules).
- **Composition** (three types of members):
  - **Ex officio:** the **Director General of Health Services (chairman)**, the **Drugs Controller General of India**, the Director of the **Central Drugs Laboratory**, Kolkata, the Director of the **Central Research Institute**, Kasauli, the Director of the **Indian Veterinary Research Institute**, Izatnagar, and the heads of certain other bodies named in the Act (such as the President of the Pharmacy Council of India).
  - **Nominated** by the Central Government, including persons in charge of drug control in the States and a person from the pharmaceutical industry.
  - **Elected** by professional bodies, including a **teacher of pharmacy** (elected by the Executive Committee of the PCI), a **teacher of medicine or therapeutics**, a **pharmacologist** (elected by the governing body of the ICMR), and representatives of the medical and pharmaceutical associations.
- Nominated and elected members hold office for **three years** and can be re-nominated or re-elected. Some bodies named in the Act (for example, the Medical Council of India) have since been replaced; check the current composition.

### Central Drugs Laboratory (CDL) — section 6

- Located at **Kolkata**; certain classes of drugs are tested at other notified central laboratories (for example, vaccines and sera at the Central Research Institute, Kasauli).
- **Functions:** analysis of samples sent by customs and drugs inspectors; **appellate (referee) testing** when a manufacturer disputes a Government Analyst's report — the CDL report is **final**; preparation of reference standards; advice on quality standards.

### Drugs Consultative Committee (DCC) — section 7

- **Composition:** **two representatives of the Central Government** and **one representative of each State Government**.
- **Function:** to secure **uniformity** in the administration of the Act throughout India; advises the Central Government, State Governments and the DTAB.
- Meets when called by the Central Government; regulates its own procedure.

### Government Analysts — section 20

- Appointed by the Central or State Government for notified areas and classes of drugs.
- Must have the qualifications laid down in the rules (degree in medicine, science or pharmacy with specified experience in drug testing); must have **no financial interest** in the import, manufacture or sale of drugs.
- **Duties:** analyse samples sent by inspectors or others and give a **report in the prescribed form** to the inspector; send reports to the Government.

### Licensing authorities

- **Central:** the **Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI)**, head of CDSCO — import licences, new drug permissions, clinical trials, Central Licence Approving Authority for Schedule C/C(1) items, vaccines and blood products.
- **State:** the **State Drugs Controller** (licensing authority) — manufacturing licences for most drugs and all sale licences.

### Controlling authority

The officer appointed by the State Government (usually the State Drugs Controller) to **control and supervise** the work of drugs inspectors, approve prosecutions and take action on reports.

### Drugs Inspectors — sections 21 to 23

**Qualifications:** a degree in pharmacy or pharmaceutical sciences or medicine (with clinical pharmacology or microbiology), as the rules require; for inspecting the manufacture of Schedule C items, additional experience is needed. An inspector must have **no financial interest** in the drug trade.

**Powers (section 22):**

1. **Inspect** premises where drugs or cosmetics are manufactured, stored, sold or distributed.
2. **Take samples** of any drug or cosmetic.
3. **Search** any person, place or vehicle believed to hold drugs in breach of the Act.
4. **Stop and search** vehicles, and **enter and search** premises.
5. **Seize** drugs, cosmetics, records and materials used in breach of the Act, and **examine records**.
6. Require production of documents.

**Procedure for taking a sample (section 23):**

```text
Inspector pays the fair price and gives a written receipt
      |
Divides the sample into 4 portions, seals and marks each
      |
 1 portion -> person from whom taken
 1 portion -> Government Analyst for test
 1 portion -> court (if prosecution)
 1 portion -> manufacturer (if named on the label)
```

**Duties:** inspect licensed premises regularly (generally at least once or twice a year as directed), check compliance with licence conditions, send samples for test, investigate complaints, institute prosecutions with sanction of the controlling authority, and maintain records of inspections.

## Remember

- **G** = caution label; **H** = Rx; **H1** = Rx in red + register (3 years); **X** = XRx, duplicate prescription (2 years), lock and key.
- **M** = GMP (revised Dec 2023); **N** = pharmacy minimum equipment; **P** = shelf life (P1 = pack sizes); **T** = ASU GMP; **U** = manufacturing and analytical records; **V** = vitamin/mineral standards for patent medicines; **Y** = clinical trials, now **NDCT Rules 2019**; **Part XII B / Sch F** = blood centres.
- Sale licences: 20/21 retail, 20B/21B wholesale, 20F/20G Schedule X, 20A/21A restricted; retail premises **10 m²**, combined **15 m²**.
- Labels: generic name, content, batch, licence no., Mfg and Exp dates, MRP, maker's address, schedule warnings.
- **DTAB** (s.5, chairman DGHS) = technical advice; **CDL** (s.6, Kolkata) = final appellate test; **DCC** (s.7, 2 Central + 1 per State) = uniformity; **Government Analyst** (s.20); **Inspector** (s.21–23) with powers to inspect, sample, search and seize.
