# Unit 3: Pharmacy Act, 1948; Medicinal and Toilet Preparations Act, 1955; NDPS Act, 1985

This unit has three Acts. The **Pharmacy Act, 1948** regulates the **profession** of pharmacy. The **Medicinal and Toilet Preparations (Excise Duties) Act, 1955** dealt with the **excise duty** on alcohol- and narcotic-containing preparations (it has been repealed — see 3.2). The **Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985** controls **narcotic and psychotropic** drugs. It is a large unit; learn the Pharmacy Act and NDPS Act in full, and the M&TP Act in outline.

## 3.1 Pharmacy Act, 1948

### Objectives

1. To **regulate the profession and practice of pharmacy** in India.
2. To set up the **Pharmacy Council of India (PCI)** and **State Pharmacy Councils**.
3. To lay down **minimum standards of pharmacy education** (Education Regulations) and approve institutions and courses.
4. To provide for **registration of pharmacists** and maintenance of registers.
5. To make sure that only **registered pharmacists** compound and dispense medicines (where the State has notified this).

### Important definitions

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Central Council | The Pharmacy Council of India constituted under section 3 |
| State Council | A State Pharmacy Council constituted under section 19 |
| Joint State Council | A council formed by agreement between two or more States (section 20) |
| Registered pharmacist | A person whose name is entered in the register of pharmacists of the State in which he is residing or carrying on the business or profession of pharmacy |
| Register | The register of pharmacists maintained by a State Council |
| Medical practitioner | A person registered under the law relating to medical registration (now under the National Medical Commission system) |
| Education Regulations | Regulations made under section 10 |

### Pharmacy Council of India — constitution (section 3)

| Clause | Members |
| --- | --- |
| (a) | **Six** members elected by the **University Grants Commission** from among teachers of pharmacy, with at least one teacher each of **pharmaceutical chemistry, pharmacy, pharmacology and pharmacognosy** |
| (b) | **Six** members **nominated by the Central Government**, of whom at least **four** hold a degree or diploma in pharmacy or pharmaceutical chemistry, or are registered pharmacists |
| (c) | **One** member elected by the **Medical Council of India** from among its members (the MCI has since been replaced by the National Medical Commission) |
| (d) | The **Director General of Health Services**, ex officio |
| (dd) | The **Drugs Controller of India**, ex officio |
| (e) | The **Director of the Central Drugs Laboratory**, ex officio |
| (f) | **One representative each** of the **UGC** and the **AICTE** |
| (g) | **One registered pharmacist from each State**, elected by the State Pharmacy Council from among its members |
| (h) | **One member from each State**, nominated by the State Government, who is a registered pharmacist |

- The **President and Vice-President** are elected by the members from among themselves.
- Elected and nominated members normally hold office for **five years** and may be re-elected or re-nominated.
- An **Executive Committee** (President and Vice-President as ex officio members, with other members) carries out the Council's work between meetings.
- A **Secretary/Registrar** and staff are appointed by the Council.

### Functions of the PCI

1. **Education Regulations (section 10):** prescribe the **minimum standard of education** for registration as a pharmacist — nature and period of study and practical training, subjects of examination, equipment and facilities, and conditions of admission. They need the approval of the Central Government (examples: D.Pharm Education Regulations, 2020; B.Pharm Course Regulations, 2014; Pharm.D Regulations, 2008).
2. **Approval of courses and institutions (section 12):** an institution or examination that meets the Education Regulations is approved; only approved qualifications lead to registration.
3. **Withdrawal of approval (section 13)** if standards are not maintained, after inspection and a chance to explain.
4. **Inspection** of institutions and examinations through inspectors.
5. **Qualifications granted outside India (section 14):** recognition on a reciprocal basis.
6. **Central Register of Pharmacists (section 15A):** compiled from State registers.
7. Framing other regulations, for example the **Pharmacy Practice Regulations, 2015** (duties of pharmacists, code of ethics, record of prescriptions).
8. Advising the Government on pharmacy education and practice.

### State Pharmacy Councils (section 19)

| Clause | Members |
| --- | --- |
| (a) | **Six** members elected by **registered pharmacists** of the State from among themselves |
| (b) | **Five** members **nominated by the State Government**, of whom at least **three** hold a degree or diploma in pharmacy or pharmaceutical chemistry or are registered pharmacists |
| (c) | **One** member elected by the **State Medical Council** from among its members |
| (d) | The **chief administrative medical officer** of the State, ex officio |
| (dd) | The **officer in charge of drugs control** of the State, ex officio |
| (e) | The **Government Analyst** under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, ex officio (one chosen by the State if there are several) |

**Joint State Council (section 20):** two or more States (or a State and Union Territories) may agree to have one joint council; the agreement fixes the share of members and expenses.

**Functions of a State Council:**

1. Prepare and maintain the **register of pharmacists** of the State.
2. **Register** qualified persons, issue certificates and collect fees.
3. **Remove or restore** names in the register.
4. Appoint **Registrar** and **inspectors (section 26A)** to inspect premises where drugs are compounded or dispensed, check that a registered pharmacist is in charge, and investigate complaints.
5. Run continuing education and maintain discipline of the profession.

### Registration of pharmacists

```text
First register (section 29-31)
  -> prepared when the Act was first applied in a State; persons with
     the qualifications or experience listed in section 31 were entered

Subsequent registration (section 32)
  -> age 18 years or more
  -> holds an approved qualification (e.g. D.Pharm / B.Pharm under the
     Education Regulations)
  -> pays the prescribed fee
  -> name entered, certificate of registration issued

Renewal (section 34) -> fee as laid down; name removed if not renewed
Removal (section 36) -> misconduct, conviction for an offence, wrong entry,
                        after an inquiry and a chance to be heard
Restoration (section 37) -> on application and fee, if the Council agrees
```

### Offences and penalties

| Section | Offence |
| --- | --- |
| 26A | **Obstructing an inspector** or refusing information |
| 41 | **Falsely claiming to be registered**, or using the title "pharmacist" or letters suggesting registration when not registered |
| 42 | **Dispensing by an unregistered person**: after a date notified by the State Government, no one other than a registered pharmacist may compound, prepare, mix or dispense a medicine on the prescription of a medical practitioner (a doctor dispensing for his own patients is exempt) |
| 43 | **Failure to surrender the certificate of registration** after the name is removed |

**Penalties — check the current text.** In the original Act (the version in most textbooks), section 42 carried imprisonment up to **six months**, or fine up to **₹1,000**, or both; section 41 carried a fine up to **₹500** for the first offence and imprisonment or a higher fine for later offences; section 43 carried a small fine. The **Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023** amended these penalty sections (26A, 41, 42 and 43) — in force from **31 December 2024** — largely replacing short prison terms with much **larger monetary penalties**, and inserted **section 43A** for penalties to be imposed by an **adjudicating officer**. Learn the present figures from the latest bare Act or PCI notices before the exam.

## 3.2 Medicinal and Toilet Preparations (Excise Duties) Act, 1955

> **Repealed.** This Act was repealed by **section 174(1) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017**, with effect from **1 July 2017**, when GST came in. Alcohol-based medicinal and toilet preparations are now taxed under GST. The PCI syllabus still lists the Act, so learn its outline and always add a line in your answer that it stands repealed. Check whether your university still asks it.

### Objectives (when in force)

1. To provide for the **levy and collection of excise duty** on medicinal and toilet preparations containing **alcohol, opium, Indian hemp or other narcotic drugs**.
2. To have **uniform rates** of duty throughout India (the Act was a Central law, but duties were collected by the **State excise departments**).
3. To prevent misuse of duty-free alcohol by **supervising manufacture**.

### Definitions

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Alcohol | Ethyl alcohol (C2H5OH) of any strength and purity |
| Dutiable goods | Medicinal and toilet preparations listed in the Schedule to the Act |
| Medicinal preparation | A drug that is a remedy or prescription prepared for internal or external use of human beings or animals, and includes Ayurvedic, homoeopathic and allopathic preparations |
| Toilet preparation | A preparation for use in the toilet of the human body or in perfumery (for example, hair oils, lotions, perfumes, mouthwashes) |
| Narcotic drug | Includes opium, cocaine, Indian hemp and their derivatives |
| Bonded manufactory | Premises where dutiable goods are made **under excise supervision** without prior payment of duty on the alcohol used |

### Licensing

- A **licence** from the State excise authority was needed to manufacture any dutiable goods, and the manufacturer also needed a drug manufacturing licence under the D&C Act.
- Licences covered manufacture in bond, manufacture outside bond, bonded warehouses, and wholesale of preparations containing narcotic drugs.

### Manufacture in bond and outside bond

| Point | In bond | Outside bond |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alcohol used | Supplied **without duty** | **Duty-paid** alcohol bought by the maker |
| Duty paid | When finished goods are **removed** from the manufactory | Already paid on the alcohol; extra duty as laid down |
| Supervision | Constant **excise officer** supervision; locks and stock registers | Periodic checks |
| Used for | Preparations **capable of being consumed as ordinary alcoholic beverages** ("restricted preparations") had to be made in bond | Preparations **not capable** of being drunk as a beverage ("unrestricted") could be made outside bond |

### Export of alcoholic preparations

Dutiable goods could be **exported without payment of duty** (under bond, with proof of export) or with **rebate** of the duty paid, so that Indian products remained competitive abroad.

### Ayurvedic, homoeopathic and patent or proprietary preparations

- **Ayurvedic** preparations such as **asavas and arishtas** contain **alcohol formed by their own fermentation**; the Act set conditions and duty for them, with special treatment where they were not capable of being consumed as ordinary alcoholic beverages.
- **Homoeopathic** preparations (mother tinctures and potencies) are made in alcohol; they were manufactured under licence and excise supervision.
- **Patent or proprietary** allopathic preparations containing alcohol (for example, tonics and cough syrups) carried duty according to their class.

### Offences and penalties

Manufacture without a licence, removal of goods without paying duty, use of duty-free alcohol for other purposes, and false accounts were offences punishable with **fine, imprisonment and confiscation** of the goods. Exact amounts are no longer relevant after the repeal.

## 3.3 Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 and Rules

### Background and objectives

- Came into force in **November 1985**, replacing the **Opium Acts (1857, 1878)** and the **Dangerous Drugs Act, 1930**. Amended in **1989, 2001, 2014 and 2021**.
- Gives effect to India's obligations under the UN conventions on narcotic drugs (1961), psychotropic substances (1971) and illicit traffic (1988).

**Objectives**

1. To consolidate and amend the law on narcotic drugs.
2. To make **stringent provisions** for control and regulation of operations relating to narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances.
3. To provide for **forfeiture of property** derived from illicit traffic.
4. To implement international conventions.
5. To permit use **only for medical and scientific purposes**, and to support treatment and rehabilitation of addicts.

### Important definitions

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Addict | A person dependent on any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance |
| Cannabis (hemp) | **Charas** (separated resin), **ganja** (flowering or fruiting tops, excluding seeds and leaves not accompanied by tops), and any mixture of them |
| Coca derivative | Crude cocaine, ecgonine, cocaine and their preparations |
| Opium | The coagulated juice of the opium poppy, and mixtures of it |
| Opium derivative | Medicinal opium, prepared opium, phenanthrene alkaloids (morphine, codeine, thebaine) and their salts, diacetylmorphine (heroin) |
| Poppy straw | All parts of the opium poppy after harvesting, except the seeds |
| Manufactured drug | Coca derivatives, medicinal hemp, opium derivatives, poppy straw concentrate, and other drugs declared by the Government |
| Narcotic drug | Coca leaf, cannabis, opium, poppy straw and all manufactured drugs |
| Psychotropic substance | Any substance, natural or synthetic, in the **list in the Schedule** to the Act (for example, diazepam, alprazolam, amphetamine, LSD) |
| Essential narcotic drug | A narcotic drug notified by the Central Government for medical and scientific use (added in **2014** to make morphine, fentanyl, methadone and similar drugs easier to get for **pain relief and palliative care** under uniform central rules) |
| Small / commercial quantity | Quantities **notified by the Central Government** for each drug; they decide the punishment |
| Controlled substance | A chemical (precursor) used to make narcotic drugs or psychotropic substances, regulated under section 9A |

### Authorities and officers

| Section | Authority | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | **Central Government** | Takes all measures for prevention and combating of abuse and illicit traffic; may constitute an authority — the **Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB)** was set up in 1986 |
| 5 | **Narcotics Commissioner** and other officers | Supervises **opium poppy cultivation and opium production**; heads the **Central Bureau of Narcotics** |
| 6 | **NDPS Consultative Committee** | Advises the Central Government |
| 7 | Officers of State Governments | Appointed by the States for their duties under the Act |
| 7A | **National Fund for Control of Drug Abuse** | See below |

### Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Consultative Committee (section 6)

- **Constitution:** set up by the Central Government by notification; a **Chairman** and other members **not exceeding twenty**, appointed by the Central Government.
- **Function:** to **advise the Central Government** on matters relating to the administration of the Act that are referred to it.
- It may form **sub-committees**, which may include persons who are not members.
- Meets when required and regulates its own procedure.

### National Fund for Controlling Drug Abuse (section 7A, inserted in 1989)

- Constituted by the Central Government; money comes from **sale proceeds of property forfeited** under the Act, **grants** from any person or institution, and income from investment of the fund.
- **Used for:**
  1. Combating illicit traffic in narcotic drugs.
  2. Controlling abuse of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances.
  3. Identifying, treating and **rehabilitating addicts**.
  4. **Preventing drug abuse** and **educating the public**.
  5. Supplying drugs to addicts where this is medically necessary.

### Prohibition, control and regulation (sections 8 to 9A)

**Section 8** — no person shall:

1. **Cultivate** any coca plant, opium poppy or cannabis plant;
2. **Produce, manufacture, possess, sell, purchase, transport, warehouse, use, consume, import inter-State, export inter-State, import into India, export from India or tranship** any narcotic drug or psychotropic substance;

**except for medical or scientific purposes** and in the manner and to the extent allowed by the Act, rules and licences.

**Section 9 — powers of the Central Government** to permit, control and regulate: cultivation of the **opium poppy**, production of **opium** and **poppy straw**, manufacture of opium and manufactured drugs, sale of opium to manufacturers, **import and export**, and the use of psychotropic substances.

**Section 9A** — control of **controlled substances** (precursor chemicals such as acetic anhydride, ephedrine, pseudoephedrine).

**Section 10 — powers of State Governments** (by rules) to regulate: possession, transport, purchase and sale of poppy straw; possession, transport, use and sale of **manufactured drugs other than prepared opium** (except essential narcotic drugs, which are now centrally regulated); and **cultivation of cannabis** (except charas).

### Opium poppy cultivation and production of poppy straw

```text
Central Government notifies tracts (parts of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and
Uttar Pradesh) and the licensing policy each crop year
      |
Narcotics Commissioner grants LICENCES to cultivators
      |
Cultivator grows poppy in the licensed area, lances the capsules
      |
All opium collected is TENDERED to the Central Bureau of Narcotics
at the price fixed by Government (a minimum yield is required to keep the licence)
      |
Opium processed at Government Opium and Alkaloid Works (Ghazipur, Neemuch)
      |
Medicinal opium, morphine, codeine, thebaine -> licensed makers / export
```

- **Poppy straw** left after harvest is controlled; its possession, transport and sale are regulated by the States under licence. In recent years Government has also permitted production of **concentrate of poppy straw** under strict control.
- India is one of the countries recognised for **licit opium production** for medical use.

### Manufacture, sale and export of opium

- **Manufacture** of opium and of opium alkaloids from raw opium is done in **Government factories** (Government Opium and Alkaloid Works) under the Central Government.
- **Sale** of opium to licensed manufacturers of medicines is controlled by the Central Government.
- **Export** of opium is done **only by or on behalf of the Central Government**, under international control (import certificates of the importing country).
- Manufactured drugs and psychotropic substances are made and sold by private firms only under licences under the NDPS Rules and the D&C Act, with records and returns.

### Offences and penalties

**Offences by substance (sections 15 to 22):** poppy straw (15), coca plant and coca leaves (16), prepared opium (17), opium poppy and opium (18), embezzlement of opium by a licensed cultivator (19), cannabis (20), manufactured drugs (21), psychotropic substances (22), illegal import, export or transhipment (23), external dealings (24), allowing premises to be used (25), contraventions by licensees (26).

**Graded punishment by quantity (since 2001):**

| Quantity involved | Punishment (as in sections 15–22) |
| --- | --- |
| **Small quantity** | Rigorous imprisonment up to **1 year** (six months before the 2014 amendment), or fine up to **₹10,000**, or both |
| More than small but **less than commercial** | Rigorous imprisonment up to **10 years** and fine up to **₹1 lakh** |
| **Commercial quantity** | Rigorous imprisonment **10 to 20 years** and fine **₹1 lakh to ₹2 lakh** (the court may impose a higher fine, giving reasons) |

Examples of notified quantities (small / commercial): heroin 5 g / 250 g; opium 25 g / 2.5 kg; ganja 1 kg / 20 kg; charas 100 g / 1 kg; cocaine 2 g / 100 g. Check the current notification.

**Other important provisions:**

| Section | Provision |
| --- | --- |
| 27 | **Consumption**: for cocaine, morphine, diacetylmorphine or other notified drugs — imprisonment up to **1 year** or fine up to **₹20,000** or both; for other drugs — up to **6 months** or fine up to **₹10,000** or both |
| 27A | **Financing illicit traffic and harbouring offenders** — rigorous imprisonment **10 to 20 years** and fine **₹1 to 2 lakh** (a 2021 amendment corrected the cross-reference in this section) |
| 28, 29 | **Attempt, abetment and criminal conspiracy** — same punishment as the offence |
| 31 | **Repeat offence** — up to **one and a half times** the maximum punishment |
| 31A | **Death penalty** for certain repeat offences involving large quantities; since **2014** the court may instead give the punishment under section 31 |
| 32 | Offences with no specific penalty — imprisonment up to 6 months, or fine, or both |
| 35 | Court presumes a **culpable mental state**; the accused must prove otherwise |
| 36 | **Special Courts** |
| 37 | Serious offences are **cognizable** and bail is restricted |
| 64A | **Immunity from prosecution** for an addict charged with consumption or a small-quantity offence who **volunteers for treatment** at a recognised centre |
| 68A–68Y | **Forfeiture of property** derived from illicit traffic |

### NDPS Rules

- **NDPS Rules, 1985** (Central) cover cultivation, opium manufacture, import and export, manufactured drugs, psychotropic substances and **essential narcotic drugs**; **State NDPS Rules** cover possession, transport and sale within a State.
- Pharmacies stocking narcotic drugs need the required licence, keep **records** of receipt and sale in the prescribed registers, dispense only on prescription, and file returns.

## Remember

- **Pharmacy Act 1948:** PCI under **section 3** (6 UGC-elected teachers + 6 Central nominees + 1 MCI + DGHS + DCI + Director CDL + UGC and AICTE reps + 1 elected and 1 nominated per State); **section 10** Education Regulations; **section 19** State Council (6 elected + 5 nominated + 1 medical council + CMO + drugs controller + Government Analyst); **section 32** registration (18 years, approved qualification, fee).
- Offences: **41** false claim, **42** unregistered dispensing, **43** not surrendering certificate, **26A** obstructing inspector — penalties changed by **Jan Vishwas Act 2023** (from 31 Dec 2024), new **section 43A** adjudication.
- **M&TP Act 1955:** excise duty on alcohol/narcotic preparations; in bond (duty-free alcohol, restricted preparations) vs outside bond (duty-paid); **repealed by section 174 of the CGST Act, 2017, from 1 July 2017**.
- **NDPS 1985:** s.4 Central Govt (NCB), s.5 Narcotics Commissioner, **s.6 Consultative Committee (Chairman + up to 20)**, **s.7A National Fund (1989)**, s.8 prohibition, s.9 Central powers, s.10 State powers.
- Opium: licensed cultivation → tender to Government → Government Opium and Alkaloid Works (Ghazipur, Neemuch) → export only by Government.
- Punishment by quantity: small (up to 1 year), intermediate (up to 10 years), commercial (10–20 years); s.27 consumption; s.31A death penalty now discretionary; s.64A immunity for addicts seeking treatment.

# Unit 4: Drugs and Magic Remedies Act, Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, NPPA and DPCO 2013

This unit covers three different kinds of control: control of **advertisements** of drugs and remedies (DMR Act), control of **experiments on animals** (PCA Act and the CPCSEA/CCSEA system), and control of **drug prices** (NPPA, DPCO 2013 and the National List of Essential Medicines).

## 4.1 Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act, 1954 and Rules, 1955

### Objectives

1. To **control advertisements of drugs** in certain cases.
2. To **prohibit advertisements of remedies alleged to have magic qualities**.
3. To stop people from being misled into **self-medication** with harmful or useless remedies, and to protect them from **quackery** for serious diseases.

### Definitions

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Advertisement** | Any notice, circular, label, wrapper or other document, and any announcement made **orally or by any means** of producing or transmitting light, sound or smoke (today this covers print, radio, TV, internet and social media) |
| **Drug** | A medicine for internal or external use of human beings or animals; a substance meant for diagnosis, treatment, mitigation or prevention of disease; an article (other than food) meant to affect the organic functions of the body; any article meant as a component of these |
| **Magic remedy** | Includes a **talisman, mantra, kavacha, charm** or any other article which is claimed to have **miraculous powers** for curing, diagnosing, preventing or mitigating disease, or affecting the structure or function of the body |
| **Registered medical practitioner** | A person registered under the medical registration laws (including Indian systems of medicine) |
| **Taking part in the publication** | Includes printing, publishing, distributing or otherwise circulating an advertisement |

### Prohibition of certain advertisements

**Section 3** — no person shall take part in publishing an advertisement referring to a drug in terms that suggest or are meant to lead to its use for:

1. **Procuring miscarriage** in women or **preventing conception**;
2. **Maintenance or improvement of the capacity of human beings for sexual pleasure**;
3. **Correction of menstrual disorder** in women;
4. **Diagnosis, cure, mitigation, treatment or prevention** of any disease, disorder or condition **listed in the Schedule** to the Act.

The **Schedule** lists **54** diseases and conditions, for example: appendicitis, arteriosclerosis, blindness, cancer, cataract, deafness, diabetes, epilepsy, glaucoma, goitre, hernia, high or low blood pressure, leucoderma, paralysis, sexual impotence, premature ageing and venereal diseases.

**Section 4 — misleading advertisements.** No advertisement of a drug may contain matter that **directly or indirectly gives a false impression** about the true character of the drug, makes a **false claim** for it, or is otherwise **false or misleading** in any material particular.

**Section 5 — magic remedies.** No person shall take part in publishing any advertisement referring to a **magic remedy** that directly or indirectly claims it can cure, diagnose, prevent or mitigate any disease (or any Schedule condition).

**Section 6 — import and export** into or out of India of documents containing such advertisements is prohibited.

### Classes of exempted advertisements (section 14)

The Act does **not** apply to:

1. A **signboard or notice** displayed by a registered medical practitioner on his premises indicating that treatment for any disease is given there.
2. A **treatise or book** dealing with any of the matters in section 3 from a bona fide scientific or social standpoint.
3. Any advertisement relating to a drug **sent confidentially** to registered medical practitioners (and as the rules allow, to chemists, hospitals and laboratories), with the words "For the use only of registered medical practitioners or a hospital or laboratory".
4. Any advertisement **printed or published by the Government** or with its previous sanction.
5. Advertisements relating to family planning or other matters issued by Government or with its approval, and others **exempted by the Central Government** by notification.

```text
Is it an advertisement of a drug or remedy?
   |-- for a Schedule disease / sex / miscarriage / contraception / menses? --> PROHIBITED (s.3)
   |-- false or misleading?                                               --> PROHIBITED (s.4)
   |-- magic remedy claiming cure?                                        --> PROHIBITED (s.5)
   |-- exempt class under s.14 (RMP signboard, scientific book,
   |   confidential to doctors, Government)?                              --> ALLOWED
```

### Powers of entry, search and seizure (section 8)

A gazetted officer authorised by the State Government may enter and search premises, seize documents and articles believed to contravene the Act, and examine records.

### Offences and penalties (section 7)

| Offence | Punishment (as enacted) |
| --- | --- |
| **First conviction** | Imprisonment up to **six months**, or fine, or both |
| **Subsequent conviction** | Imprisonment up to **one year**, or fine, or both |

- Offences by a **company**: every person in charge of the business is liable unless he proves lack of knowledge and due diligence.
- The Ministry of Health published a **draft amendment bill in 2020** proposing much higher penalties and an updated Schedule. Check whether any amendment has been passed before quoting penalties.

### Relation with other laws

- **Schedule J** of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules prohibits **claims on the label** of a drug for listed diseases; the DMR Act prohibits **advertisements**.
- Advertising of ASU drugs is also controlled under the D&C Rules, and advertising standards are watched by the **Advertising Standards Council of India** (a self-regulatory body).

## 4.2 Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960

### Objectives

1. To **prevent the infliction of unnecessary pain or suffering** on animals.
2. To set up the **Animal Welfare Board of India**.
3. To **control and supervise experiments on animals** (Chapter IV) so that they are done only when necessary and with the least pain.

### Definitions

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Animal | Any living creature **other than a human being** |
| Captive animal | An animal (not domestic) kept in captivity or confinement, or maimed to prevent escape |
| Domestic animal | An animal tamed or being tamed for a purpose of use to man |
| Owner | Includes any person in possession or custody of the animal |
| Experiment | Use of animals for the advancement of knowledge, for saving or prolonging life, alleviating suffering, or combating disease, and for testing drugs, sera, vaccines and other biological products |

### Experiments on animals — Chapter IV (sections 14 to 20)

- **Section 14:** nothing in the Act makes it unlawful to perform experiments on animals for the advancement of knowledge (physiological, medical, veterinary) that will save or prolong life or alleviate suffering, or for combating disease.
- **Section 15:** the Central Government constitutes a **Committee for the purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CPCSEA)** — renamed the **Committee for Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CCSEA)** in 2023. Older books and the syllabus use "CPCSEA".
- **Section 17:** duties of the Committee and its power to make rules so that animals are not subjected to unnecessary pain before, during or after experiments.
- **Section 18:** power of the Committee to **inspect** establishments where experiments are done.
- **Section 19:** **power to prohibit** experiments, or to **suspend or revoke** the registration of an institution, if rules are not followed.
- **Section 20:** **penalties** for breaking the Committee's orders or conditions (a fine under the original Act).

The **Breeding of and Experiments on Animals (Control and Supervision) Rules, 1998** (amended later) give the details.

### Main provisions of the CPCSEA (CCSEA) system

**1. Registration of establishments**

Every institution that **breeds, trades in or uses** animals for experiments must be **registered** with the Committee; registration is renewed periodically.

**2. Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (IAEC)**

Every registered establishment must set up an **IAEC**, approved by the Committee. Its members include:

| Member | Role |
| --- | --- |
| Biological scientist | Chairs or guides scientific review |
| Scientists from different biological disciplines | Review scientific merit |
| Veterinarian | Responsible for care of the animals |
| Scientist in charge of the animal house facility | Reports on housing and husbandry |
| Scientist from outside the institute | Independent view |
| Socially aware, non-scientific member | Public interest |
| Main nominee and link nominee of the Committee | Ensure the guidelines are followed |

**Functions of the IAEC:** review and **approve protocols** for experiments on small animals; refer protocols involving **large animals** (and certain other categories) to the Committee; check that the number of animals is justified; ensure humane end points and anaesthesia or analgesia; inspect the animal house; keep records.

**3. Guidelines for breeding and stocking of animals**

- Animal house planned for the species: **separate areas** for breeding, quarantine, experimental animals, and surgery, with clean and dirty corridors.
- Controlled **temperature, humidity, light–dark cycle and ventilation**; noise control.
- Proper **caging, bedding, food and water**; space as per species and number.
- **Health monitoring**, quarantine of new arrivals, and **veterinary care**.
- **Trained staff** and personal hygiene; pest control.
- Animals should be obtained from **registered breeders**.

**4. Performance of experiments**

- Follow the **3 Rs**: **Replacement** (use non-animal methods where possible), **Reduction** (fewest animals that give valid results), **Refinement** (methods that reduce pain and distress); the Committee also stresses **Rehabilitation** of animals after experiments where possible.
- Experiments only by **qualified and trained** persons, after IAEC approval.
- Use of the **lowest species** on the phylogenetic scale that will serve the purpose.
- Proper **anaesthesia and analgesia** for painful procedures; **euthanasia** by approved humane methods when needed.
- Experiments must not be repeated unnecessarily; procedures already proven should not be repeated for demonstration where models or films will do.

**5. Transfer and acquisition of animals for experiment**

- Animals may be acquired only from **registered breeders** or other registered establishments.
- Transfer between institutions needs proper records and, where required, permission; transport in suitable conditions.

**6. Records**

Establishments keep records of **animals bred, acquired, transferred, used and disposed of**, protocols approved by the IAEC, experiments done, and veterinary care. Records are open to inspection and reports are sent to the Committee as required.

**7. Power to suspend or revoke registration**

If an establishment does not follow the rules or the conditions laid down, the Committee may, after giving a hearing, **suspend or revoke** its registration and **prohibit** it from doing experiments (section 19).

### Offences and penalties

- **Cruelty to animals (section 11):** a fine for the first offence and a higher fine or imprisonment for a repeat offence within three years. The amounts in the original Act are very small; a draft amendment proposing higher penalties has been discussed but check whether it has been passed.
- **Contravening an order under section 19** or a condition imposed by the Committee is punishable under **section 20** with a fine.
- Companies and their officers are liable as the Act provides.

## 4.3 National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) and Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013

### NPPA

- Set up in **1997** under the **Department of Pharmaceuticals**, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers.
- **Functions:** fix and revise **ceiling prices** of scheduled formulations; **monitor prices** of non-scheduled formulations; enforce the DPCO; recover **overcharged amounts** from companies; monitor **availability** and shortages of medicines; advise the Government on pricing policy; collect data on production, imports and sales.

### Drugs (Prices Control) Order, 2013

- Issued by the Central Government under **section 3 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955**, based on the **National Pharmaceutical Pricing Policy, 2012**.
- Replaced **DPCO 1995**. The main change: prices are now fixed on the basis of **market prices** (market-based pricing) of **essential medicines**, instead of cost-based pricing of selected bulk drugs.

**Objectives**

1. To make **essential medicines available at reasonable prices**.
2. To keep enough room for **innovation and competition** so that the industry grows.
3. To ensure that price control does not cause **shortages**.

### Definitions (main ones)

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Scheduled formulation** | A formulation of a medicine in the **First Schedule** of the DPCO (the **NLEM**) in the same strength and dosage form |
| **Non-scheduled formulation** | A formulation not in the First Schedule |
| **Ceiling price** | The price fixed by the Government for a scheduled formulation; no one may sell above it |
| **Maximum retail price (MRP)** | The maximum price at which a drug can be sold to the consumer, inclusive of taxes |
| **Retail price** | The price fixed for a **new drug** (see below) |
| **Price to retailer (PTR)** | The price at which a drug is sold to the retailer, including taxes |
| **Moving annual turnover** | Sales value of a product over the preceding twelve months, used to decide market share |
| **New drug** (for DPCO) | A formulation launched by an existing manufacturer of a scheduled drug by combining it with another drug or by changing its strength or dosage form |
| **Bulk drug (API)** | Any pharmaceutical, chemical, biological or plant product used as an active ingredient in a formulation |
| **Wholesale price index (WPI)** | The index published by the Government used for annual revision of ceiling prices |

### Sale prices of bulk drugs

DPCO 2013 does **not** routinely fix prices of bulk drugs (DPCO 1995 did). The Government can, however, direct manufacturers of a bulk drug used in scheduled formulations to **maintain supply** to formulation makers, and may fix its price in special circumstances to ensure availability.

### Calculation of ceiling price of a scheduled formulation

```text
Step 1  Take all brands and generic versions of the formulation that have
        market share of 1% or more of the total market turnover of that medicine.
Step 2  Find each one's price to retailer (PTR).
Step 3  Take the SIMPLE AVERAGE of these PTRs.
Step 4  Add a RETAILER MARGIN of 16% to the average.
                Ceiling price = Average PTR x 1.16  (taxes extra as allowed)
```

**Worked example**

| Brand | Market share | PTR per 10 tablets (₹) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 30% | 20.00 |
| B | 20% | 24.00 |
| C | 10% | 16.00 |
| D | 0.5% | 40.00 (left out, share below 1%) |

Average PTR = (20 + 24 + 16) ÷ 3 = ₹20.00 → ceiling price = 20.00 × 1.16 = **₹23.20** per 10 tablets.

- Manufacturers selling **above** the ceiling price must **reduce** their price to the ceiling; those selling **below** must **not increase** it (except for the annual WPI increase).
- **Annual revision:** ceiling prices are revised every year on **1 April** in line with the **WPI** change for the previous calendar year (paragraph 16).

### Retail price of formulations and of a new drug

- For a **new drug** (as defined above) the manufacturer must apply, and the Government fixes its **retail price** using the market-based method on comparable formulations; the drug cannot be launched at a higher price.
- Every manufacturer must print the **MRP** on the label and issue a **price list** to dealers; retailers must display the price list and must not sell above the MRP or ceiling price.

### Non-scheduled formulations

- Prices are **monitored**; a manufacturer may not raise the MRP by more than **10% in a twelve-month period**. Excess must be reduced.

### Other important provisions

- **Paragraph 19** — the Government may, in **extraordinary circumstances** and in public interest, fix the ceiling or retail price of any drug for a stated period (used, for example, for cardiac stents and for trade-margin capping of certain cancer drugs).
- **Overcharging:** amounts charged above the notified price are **recovered with interest** under the Essential Commodities Act.
- **Discontinuation:** a manufacturer of a scheduled formulation intending to stop production must give **six months' notice**.
- **Exemptions:** certain patented drugs and drugs from new delivery systems or indigenous research may be exempted for a period as the Order allows.
- **Penalties:** contravention of the DPCO is punishable under the **Essential Commodities Act, 1955**.

### National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM)

- **Essential medicines** are those that satisfy the **priority health care needs** of the population, chosen for **efficacy, safety and cost-effectiveness**, and are meant to be available at all times in adequate amounts and affordable prices.
- India's lists: 1996, 2003, 2011, 2015 and **NLEM 2022** (released September 2022; **384 medicines** in **27 therapeutic categories**).
- NLEM 2022 forms the **First Schedule of the DPCO 2013**, so medicines in it come under **price control**.
- Medicines are listed by **generic name**, with dosage form and strength, and the level of health care (primary, secondary, tertiary).
- Criteria include: proven efficacy and safety, relevance to public health in India, cost-effectiveness, approval in India, and preference for single-ingredient medicines; fixed-dose combinations only where proven useful.

## Remember

- **DMR Act 1954:** s.3 bans adverts for miscarriage, contraception, sexual pleasure, menstrual disorders and **54 Schedule diseases**; s.4 misleading adverts; s.5 **magic remedies** (talisman, mantra, kavacha, charm); s.14 exemptions; s.7 penalty **6 months / 1 year** as enacted.
- **PCA Act 1960:** Chapter IV (s.14–20); **CPCSEA → CCSEA (2023)**; Rules 1998; IAEC; registration, 3 Rs, records, power to suspend or revoke registration (s.19), penalty (s.20).
- **NPPA (1997)** enforces **DPCO 2013** (under s.3 of the **Essential Commodities Act, 1955**; based on NPPP 2012).
- Ceiling price = **simple average PTR of brands with ≥1% share + 16% retailer margin**; revised yearly on **1 April** by **WPI**; non-scheduled drugs **≤10%** rise per year; para 19 for extraordinary circumstances.
- **NLEM 2022:** 384 medicines, 27 categories = First Schedule of DPCO 2013.

# Unit 5: Pharmaceutical legislation history, code of ethics, MTP Act, RTI Act and IPR

This last unit is shorter in hours but full of short-answer questions: the **history of pharmaceutical legislation** and the committees behind it, the **Code of Pharmaceutical Ethics** and the pharmacist's oath, the **Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act**, the **Right to Information Act** and an **introduction to intellectual property rights**.

## 5.1 Pharmaceutical legislation in India — a brief review

### Why pharmaceutical laws are needed

- Medicines can **heal or harm**; the public cannot judge their quality by looking at them.
- Without control, **spurious and substandard** drugs, **misleading advertisements** and **unqualified sellers** flourish.
- Laws protect the public, set standards for education and practice, control **habit-forming drugs**, keep **prices** reasonable, and meet **international obligations**.

### Timeline

| Year | Law or event |
| --- | --- |
| 1857, 1878 | **Opium Acts** (control of opium cultivation and trade) |
| 1919 | **Poisons Act** (control of import, possession and sale of poisons) |
| 1930 | **Dangerous Drugs Act**; **Drugs Enquiry Committee** appointed |
| 1940 | **Drugs Act** (later Drugs and Cosmetics Act) |
| 1945 | **Drugs Rules** (later Drugs and Cosmetics Rules) |
| 1946 | Report of the **Health Survey and Development Committee** (Bhore) |
| 1948 | **Pharmacy Act** |
| 1954 | **Drugs and Magic Remedies (Objectionable Advertisements) Act** |
| 1955 | **Medicinal and Toilet Preparations (Excise Duties) Act**; **Essential Commodities Act** |
| 1960 | **Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act** |
| 1961 | Report of the **Health Survey and Planning Committee** (Mudaliar) |
| 1970 | **Patents Act** (process patents only for drugs) |
| 1971 | **Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act** |
| 1975 | Report of the **Hathi Committee** |
| 1985 | **NDPS Act** |
| 1997 | **NPPA** set up |
| 2005 | **Right to Information Act**; product patents for drugs (Patents Amendment Act) |
| 2013 | **DPCO 2013** |
| 2017 | **Medical Devices Rules**; **M&TP Act repealed** with GST |
| 2019 | **New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules** |

### Drugs Enquiry Committee (1930–31)

- Appointed by the Government of India in **1930** under the chairmanship of **Col. R. N. Chopra**, to enquire into the extent of sale of **substandard and adulterated drugs** and to suggest remedies. Report in **1931**.
- **Findings:** a large quantity of substandard, adulterated and spurious drugs on the market; no control on import, manufacture or sale; dispensing and sale by unqualified people; no pharmacy profession as such.
- **Main recommendations:**
  1. A **central law** to control the import, manufacture, distribution and sale of drugs.
  2. A **Central Drugs Laboratory** and provincial laboratories for testing.
  3. **Drugs control departments** at the Centre and in the provinces with trained inspectors.
  4. Regulation of the **profession of pharmacy**: education, registration, and dispensing only by qualified persons.
  5. A **pharmacopoeia** of India and standards for drugs.
- **Results:** the **Drugs Act, 1940**, the **Pharmacy Act, 1948**, and later the Indian Pharmacopoeia.

### Health Survey and Development Committee (1943–46)

- Chaired by **Sir Joseph Bhore**; appointed in **1943**, reported in **1946** (often called the **Bhore Committee**).
- Surveyed the health conditions and organisation of India and planned future development.
- **Recommendations relevant to pharmacy:** integrate preventive and curative services; set up **primary health centres**; improve **training of health personnel**, including pharmacists; production of essential drugs in the country; proper control of drugs and dispensing.

### Health Survey and Planning Committee — Mudaliar Committee (1959–61)

- Chaired by **Dr A. Lakshmanaswami Mudaliar**; reviewed progress since the Bhore report; reported in **1961**.
- **Recommendations:** strengthen primary health centres before expanding; improve the **quality of pharmacy education** and the status of pharmacists; strengthen **drug control** at Centre and States; expand **indigenous production** of drugs; regional drug-testing laboratories.

### Hathi Committee (1974–75)

- The **Committee on Drugs and Pharmaceutical Industry**, chaired by **Jaisukhlal Hathi**, appointed in **1974**, report in **1975**.
- **Main recommendations:**
  1. Prepare a **list of essential drugs** (it listed 117 essential drugs) and give them priority in production and supply.
  2. **Promote the Indian sector**, especially public sector units, to lead the industry; reduce the dominance of foreign companies.
  3. Use of **generic names**, with brand names to be abolished in a phased manner, starting with some common drugs.
  4. Set up a **National Drug Authority** to look after drug policy, quality and prices.
  5. Strengthen **quality control** and **price control** of drugs.
  6. Encourage **research** and production of bulk drugs in India.
- These ideas shaped the **Drug Policy of 1978** and later price control.

## 5.2 Code of Pharmaceutical Ethics

### Definition

**Ethics** is the set of **moral principles** that guide the conduct of a person. A **code of pharmaceutical ethics** is the set of standards of **professional conduct** framed by the **Pharmacy Council of India** to guide pharmacists in their relations with patients, the public, the trade, the medical profession and fellow pharmacists. Many of these duties are also part of the **Pharmacy Practice Regulations, 2015**.

### Pharmacist in relation to his job

1. **Scope of service:** a pharmacy should be open for a reasonable time and should stock and supply all **necessary medicines**; emergency supply should be arranged.
2. **Conduct of the pharmacy:** clean, orderly premises; work done only by or under a **registered pharmacist**.
3. **Handling of prescriptions:** check the prescription; **do not change** it without the prescriber's consent; if an error or overdose is suspected, **contact the prescriber**; never discuss the prescriber's choice with the patient in a way that lowers confidence in the doctor.
4. **Dispensing:** accurate compounding, proper labelling, correct directions; use only drugs of **standard quality**.
5. **Handling of drugs:** store as labelled; take special care with **poisons, narcotic and habit-forming drugs**; do not supply them for misuse.
6. **Apprentice and staff:** train apprentices properly; supervise staff.
7. **Confidentiality:** keep patient information **secret** except where the law requires disclosure.

### Pharmacist in relation to his trade

1. **Prices** should be fair, not excessive; follow notified prices (MRP, ceiling price).
2. **No unfair competition** — no price wars, no running down of other pharmacies.
3. **No misleading advertising**; no false claims for products.
4. **Fair dealing** with suppliers and customers; honour contracts.
5. **No sale of substandard, spurious or expired** goods; no sale of habit-forming drugs without proper prescription.
6. **Hawking** of drugs (selling from door to door or in streets) should not be practised.
7. The **pharmacy's name and display** should be dignified.

### Pharmacist in relation to the medical profession

1. **Respect and cooperate** with medical practitioners; act as the doctor's partner in patient care.
2. **No counter-prescribing** or diagnosing except in genuine emergencies (first aid) — refer patients to a doctor.
3. **No secret arrangements** with doctors for **commission** or for recommending a particular pharmacy.
4. Do not **recommend a particular doctor** to patients for gain.
5. Inform the prescriber tactfully of errors in a prescription.

### Pharmacist in relation to his profession

1. Uphold the **dignity and honour** of the profession.
2. Keep up to date by **continuing education**; contribute to professional knowledge.
3. Be a member of **professional associations** and support their work.
4. Do not do anything that **brings discredit** to the profession; report unethical conduct.
5. Help **fellow pharmacists**; do not take unfair advantage of them.
6. **Obey the laws** relating to drugs and pharmacy.

### Pharmacist's oath (in substance)

A pharmacist solemnly promises to:

- Devote himself to a lifetime of **service to others** through the profession of pharmacy;
- Consider the **welfare of humanity and relief of suffering** his primary concerns;
- Apply his **knowledge, experience and skills** to the best of his ability for the best outcomes for patients;
- **Respect and protect** all personal and health information entrusted to him;
- **Keep up to date** with developments in the profession;
- Hold himself to the highest principles of **moral, ethical and legal conduct**;
- Embrace and advocate changes that **improve patient care**;
- Use his knowledge to **prevent misuse** of medicines and to promote the public's health.

## 5.3 Medical Termination of Pregnancy Act, 1971 (amended 2021)

### Objectives

1. To provide for **termination of certain pregnancies by registered medical practitioners** under safe conditions.
2. To reduce **maternal deaths and illness** caused by unsafe abortion.
3. To lay down **when, where and by whom** a pregnancy may be terminated.

### Definitions

- **Registered medical practitioner (RMP):** a medical practitioner with a recognised medical qualification, registered under the medical registration laws, and having the **experience or training in gynaecology and obstetrics** laid down by the rules.
- **Guardian:** a person who has care of a minor or a mentally ill woman.
- **Termination of pregnancy:** a procedure to end a pregnancy by medical or surgical methods.

### When a pregnancy may be terminated (as amended in 2021, in force from 24 September 2021)

| Length of pregnancy | Requirement |
| --- | --- |
| Up to **20 weeks** | Opinion of **one RMP** |
| **20 to 24 weeks** | Opinion of **two RMPs**, only for **special categories of women** notified in the rules (for example, survivors of sexual assault or incest, minors, women whose marital status changes during pregnancy, women with disabilities) |
| Beyond **24 weeks** | Only for **substantial foetal abnormalities**, on the decision of a **State Medical Board** |
| Any time | To **save the life** of the woman, on the opinion of one RMP formed in good faith |

**Grounds** (the RMP's good-faith opinion): continuing the pregnancy would risk the **life** of the woman or cause grave injury to her **physical or mental health**; or there is a substantial risk that the child would have **serious physical or mental abnormality**. Pregnancy caused by **rape** is presumed to cause grave injury to mental health; pregnancy from **failure of a contraceptive** used by **any woman or her partner** may also be treated as such (the 2021 amendment removed the earlier "married woman" limit).

### Consent

- The **woman's written consent** is required.
- For a **minor** (below 18 years) or a **mentally ill** woman, the written consent of the **guardian**.

### Place

Termination may be done only in a **Government hospital** or a place **approved** by the Government (or a District Level Committee). In an emergency to save life, it may be done elsewhere by an RMP.

### Confidentiality and penalties

- **Section 5A** (2021): the name and particulars of a woman whose pregnancy has been terminated must not be revealed except to a person authorised by law; breaking this is punishable with imprisonment up to **one year**, or fine, or both.
- Termination by a person who is not an RMP, or at an unapproved place, is an offence punishable under the **criminal law** (Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, which replaced the Indian Penal Code from July 2024).
- **Pharmacist's role:** drugs used for medical termination (for example, mifepristone with misoprostol) are prescription drugs to be sold only on an RMP's prescription and kept with records; the pharmacist must not supply them over the counter.

## 5.4 Right to Information Act, 2005

### Objectives

1. To give citizens the **right to access information** under the control of **public authorities**.
2. To promote **transparency and accountability** in government.
3. To **contain corruption** and help citizens participate in governance.

### Key definitions

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| **Information** | Any material in any form — records, documents, memos, e-mails, opinions, advice, press releases, circulars, orders, logbooks, contracts, reports, samples, models, electronic data |
| **Public authority** | Any body set up by the Constitution or by law of Parliament or a State, or by Government notification, and bodies **owned, controlled or substantially financed** by Government (including NGOs substantially financed) |
| **Right to information** | Right to inspect work, documents and records, take notes and certified copies, take **certified samples** of material, and get information in electronic form |
| **Public Information Officer (PIO)** | Officer designated in each public authority to deal with requests; **Assistant PIOs** receive requests at sub-divisional level |

### How to get information

```text
Citizen writes an application (English, Hindi or official language of the area)
   + application fee (₹10 for Central public authorities; nil for BPL card holders)
   -> PIO of the public authority (no need to give reasons)
        |
Reply within 30 days
   (48 hours if the information concerns the life or liberty of a person;
    5 more days if given to an Assistant PIO)
        |
No reply / refusal / unsatisfied
   -> First appeal to a senior officer in the same authority (within 30 days)
   -> Second appeal to the Central / State Information Commission (within 90 days)
```

### Exemptions (section 8) — main ones

Information need not be given if it would affect the **sovereignty, security** or economic interests of India; has been **forbidden by a court**; would cause **breach of privilege** of Parliament or a legislature; involves **commercial confidence, trade secrets or intellectual property** (unless larger public interest); is held in a **fiduciary** relationship; was received in confidence from a **foreign government**; would endanger **life or safety** of a person; would **impede investigation**; includes **Cabinet papers** (until decisions are taken); or is **personal information** with no relation to public activity. **Intelligence and security organisations** listed in the Second Schedule are outside the Act (section 24) except for information on corruption and human rights violations.

### Information Commissions

- **Central Information Commission:** a Chief Information Commissioner and up to ten Information Commissioners; **State Information Commissions** similarly.
- They hear complaints and appeals and can impose a **penalty on the PIO** of **₹250 per day** of delay, up to **₹25,000**, for refusing or delaying information without reasonable cause, and recommend disciplinary action.

### Proactive disclosure (section 4)

Every public authority must **publish** its organisation, functions, duties, powers of officers, rules, budget, names of PIOs and other details, and update them regularly.

### Relevance to pharmacy

Citizens and pharmacists can use RTI to get information from bodies such as **CDSCO, State Drug Controllers, NPPA and the Pharmacy Councils** (for example, licensing status, lists of banned drugs, inspection reports), subject to the exemptions. Trade secrets of a manufacturer are protected under section 8.

## 5.5 Introduction to Intellectual Property Rights (IPR)

### Meaning

**Intellectual property** is creation of the **mind** — inventions, literary and artistic works, designs, symbols, names and images used in commerce. **IPR** are legal rights that give the creator **exclusive rights** to use the creation for a **limited time**, in return for disclosure to society. Internationally they are governed by the **TRIPS Agreement** of the **World Trade Organization** (1995).

### Types of IPR in India

| Type | Indian law | What it protects | Term |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Patent** | Patents Act, 1970 | New **inventions** (products or processes) | **20 years** from the date of filing |
| **Trademark** | Trade Marks Act, 1999 | Brand names, logos, symbols that distinguish goods or services | 10 years, **renewable** indefinitely |
| **Copyright** | Copyright Act, 1957 | Literary, artistic, musical works, software | Generally the author's **lifetime + 60 years** |
| **Industrial design** | Designs Act, 2000 | Shape, pattern, ornamentation of an article (for example, a tablet shape or pack) | 10 years + 5 years extension |
| **Geographical indication** | Geographical Indications of Goods Act, 1999 | Goods identified with a place (for example, Darjeeling tea) | 10 years, renewable |
| **Trade secret** | No separate Act; protected by contracts and courts | Confidential know-how, formulae | As long as kept secret |

### Patents — key points for pharmacy

**Criteria for a patent:**

1. **Novelty** — not known or published before.
2. **Inventive step** — not obvious to a person skilled in the art; involves technical advance or economic significance.
3. **Industrial application** — can be made or used in industry.

**Not patentable (section 3) — examples:** discoveries of natural substances, methods of treatment of humans or animals, plants and animals as such (except micro-organisms), mere admixtures, and **section 3(d)** — a **new form of a known substance** (salt, ester, polymorph, isomer, etc.) is not an invention unless it shows **significantly enhanced efficacy**. The Supreme Court upheld this in the **Novartis (imatinib) case, 2013**.

**History in pharmacy:**

```text
Patents Act 1970   -> only PROCESS patents for drugs, food and chemicals
                      (term 5–7 years for these) -> growth of Indian generic industry
TRIPS (1995)       -> India given time to introduce product patents
Amendments 1999, 2002 -> mailbox applications, 20-year term
Patents (Amendment) Act 2005 -> PRODUCT patents for drugs restored; safeguards
                      like section 3(d), pre-grant opposition, compulsory licences
```

**Procedure (outline):** filing (provisional or complete specification) → publication (after 18 months) → request for examination → examination and objections → **pre-grant opposition** → grant → **post-grant opposition** (within one year) → renewal fees each year.

**Flexibilities:**

- **Compulsory licence (section 84):** after three years from grant, anyone may apply if the patented product is not available to the public at a **reasonably affordable price**, or reasonable requirements are not met, or it is not worked in India. India's first compulsory licence (2012) was for **sorafenib** (Natco vs Bayer).
- **Bolar exemption (section 107A):** using a patented invention to develop data for **regulatory approval** is not infringement, so generics can be ready when the patent expires.
- **Parallel import** of patented products under certain conditions.

### Importance of IPR for the pharmaceutical industry

- Rewards **research and development** of new drugs, which is costly and slow.
- Encourages **disclosure** of technology.
- **Brand protection** (trademarks) prevents confusion and look-alike drugs.
- Balanced with **access to medicines** through compulsory licences, 3(d) and price control.

## Remember

- **Drugs Enquiry Committee 1930–31** (Col. R. N. Chopra) → Drugs Act 1940 and Pharmacy Act 1948.
- **Bhore 1943–46** (Health Survey and Development); **Mudaliar 1959–61** (Health Survey and Planning); **Hathi 1974–75** (Drugs and Pharmaceutical Industry; essential drugs, generic names, National Drug Authority).
- Code of ethics: four relations — **job, trade, medical profession, profession**; plus the pharmacist's oath.
- **MTP Act 1971 (2021 amendment):** 20 weeks one RMP; 20–24 weeks two RMPs for special categories; beyond 24 weeks foetal abnormality via Medical Board; written consent; confidentiality under section 5A.
- **RTI Act 2005:** ₹10 fee, reply in **30 days** (48 hours for life/liberty), first appeal, second appeal to Information Commission; penalty **₹250/day up to ₹25,000**; exemptions in **section 8**.
- **IPR:** patent 20 years (novelty, inventive step, industrial use); **3(d)**; compulsory licence **s.84**; Bolar **s.107A**; trademark 10 years renewable; copyright life + 60; design 10 + 5; GI 10 renewable.
